Proposition 41: Audits For New State Special Taxes
Proposition 41: Audits For New State Special Taxes
Proposition 41: Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues From State Spending Limit. Requires Audits For New State Special Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Tax Audits, One-Time Wealth Tax for State-Funded Health Care Programs Initiative.
Improving Transparency, Effectiveness, and Efficiency in California Government Act of 2026
The Transparency Act
Summary
Proposition 41 was placed on the ballot by petition signatures to amend the California Constitution. It began as Initiative #25-0041A (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0040A1%20%28Gov.%20Efficiency%29.pdf) , filed with the California Attorney General’s Office. Prop. 41 amends the California Constitution by adding Article XXIV, creating audit review requirements for special tax measures and enforcing state appropriation limits (the Gann Limit) for all future state tax measures.
Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to conduct a financial and performance audit of any citizen initiative proposing a new special tax once the campaign collects 25% of required signatures. The auditor must review specific criteria set by Proposition 41, including identifying ways to cut the proposed program’s annual costs by 10%. If the measure qualifies, an executive summary of the audit is published in the official voter information pamphlet.
Additionally, the State Auditor will conduct ongoing audits every four years for programs receiving funding from special taxes created or increased by the Legislature or voters after January 1, 2026.
Proposition 41 specifies that the costs of these audits will be reimbursed using revenue generated from the new tax if voters approve the measure. If a special tax initiative fails, the state general fund covers the audit costs.
It would also prohibit the state from enforcing any new tax enacted or effective on or after January 1, 2026, that is exempted or excluded from the state spending limit.
Proposition 41 conflicts directly with Proposition 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/index.htm) (the Billionaire Wealth Tax initiative). If both pass, whichever measure receives more "yes" votes will prevail in its entirety. Because Proposition 40 excludes its revenues from the state spending limit, Proposition 41 would render Proposition 40 unenforceable if Proposition 41 wins more votes.
Note about the Gann Limit: Approved by California voters in 1979 asProposition 4 (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/ca_ballot_props/864/), the Gann Limit restricts how much tax revenue state and local governments (including school districts) can spend each year, adjusted annually for population changes and economic growth. The limit applies to both General Fund taxes (unrestricted funds for general government operations) and special taxes (funds earmarked for specific purposes), though certain spending categories—such as infrastructure and emergency response—are exempt. (Sources: California Budget Center, What is the Gann Limit? (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians) , Gann Limit (Wikipedia) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gann_Limit) , CA Department of Finance, Description of (https://dof.ca.gov/media/docs/budget/california-budget-frequently-asked-questions/fundclassifications.pdf)Fund Classifications in the Treasury (https://dof.ca.gov/media/docs/budget/california-budget-frequently-asked-questions/fundclassifications.pdf))
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
The net fiscal effect of Proposition 41 is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers. However, the State Auditor costs will increase due to the new and ongoing work to carry out the audit requirements in this measure.
Due to additional pages of audit information being included in the voter information guides could increase state printing and mailing costs by a few hundred thousand dollars per qualified initiative on the ballot.
What your vote means (LAO Analysis)
YES: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
NO: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that Proposition 41 improves transparency and reduces government waste by requiring independent state audits of programs funded by new special taxes while ensuring all state taxes respect voter-approved spending caps, as detailed in the Official Voter Information Guide.
Opponents contend that the measure was put on the ballot by billionaire opponents to block Prop. 40, a proposed wealth tax on billionaires, and that its audit requirements create unnecessary hurdles to funding essential public services like healthcare and education.

Proposition 41: Audits For New State Special Taxes
Proposition 41: Audits For New State Special Taxes
Proposition 41: Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues From State Spending Limit. Requires Audits For New State Special Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Tax Audits, One-Time Wealth Tax for State-Funded Health Care Programs Initiative.
Improving Transparency, Effectiveness, and Efficiency in California Government Act of 2026
The Transparency Act
Summary
Proposition 41 was placed on the ballot by petition signatures to amend the California Constitution. It began as Initiative #25-0041A (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0040A1%20%28Gov.%20Efficiency%29.pdf) , filed with the California Attorney General’s Office. Prop. 41 amends the California Constitution by adding Article XXIV, creating audit review requirements for special tax measures and enforcing state appropriation limits (the Gann Limit) for all future state tax measures.
Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to conduct a financial and performance audit of any citizen initiative proposing a new special tax once the campaign collects 25% of required signatures. The auditor must review specific criteria set by Proposition 41, including identifying ways to cut the proposed program’s annual costs by 10%. If the measure qualifies, an executive summary of the audit is published in the official voter information pamphlet.
Additionally, the State Auditor will conduct ongoing audits every four years for programs receiving funding from special taxes created or increased by the Legislature or voters after January 1, 2026.
Proposition 41 specifies that the costs of these audits will be reimbursed using revenue generated from the new tax if voters approve the measure. If a special tax initiative fails, the state general fund covers the audit costs.
It would also prohibit the state from enforcing any new tax enacted or effective on or after January 1, 2026, that is exempted or excluded from the state spending limit.
Proposition 41 conflicts directly with Proposition 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/index.htm) (the Billionaire Wealth Tax initiative). If both pass, whichever measure receives more "yes" votes will prevail in its entirety. Because Proposition 40 excludes its revenues from the state spending limit, Proposition 41 would render Proposition 40 unenforceable if Proposition 41 wins more votes.
Note about the Gann Limit: Approved by California voters in 1979 asProposition 4 (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/ca_ballot_props/864/), the Gann Limit restricts how much tax revenue state and local governments (including school districts) can spend each year, adjusted annually for population changes and economic growth. The limit applies to both General Fund taxes (unrestricted funds for general government operations) and special taxes (funds earmarked for specific purposes), though certain spending categories—such as infrastructure and emergency response—are exempt. (Sources: California Budget Center, What is the Gann Limit? (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians) , Gann Limit (Wikipedia) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gann_Limit) , CA Department of Finance, Description of (https://dof.ca.gov/media/docs/budget/california-budget-frequently-asked-questions/fundclassifications.pdf)Fund Classifications in the Treasury (https://dof.ca.gov/media/docs/budget/california-budget-frequently-asked-questions/fundclassifications.pdf))
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
The net fiscal effect of Proposition 41 is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers. However, the State Auditor costs will increase due to the new and ongoing work to carry out the audit requirements in this measure.
Due to additional pages of audit information being included in the voter information guides could increase state printing and mailing costs by a few hundred thousand dollars per qualified initiative on the ballot.
What your vote means (LAO Analysis)
YES: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
NO: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that Proposition 41 improves transparency and reduces government waste by requiring independent state audits of programs funded by new special taxes while ensuring all state taxes respect voter-approved spending caps, as detailed in the Official Voter Information Guide.
Opponents contend that the measure was put on the ballot by billionaire opponents to block Prop. 40, a proposed wealth tax on billionaires, and that its audit requirements create unnecessary hurdles to funding essential public services like healthcare and education.

​ Yes on Proposition 41: Audits and Accountability for California Tax Dollars.
​
Billions of our tax dollars have flowed into state programs like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it. Californians deserve better education, healthcare, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned money we pay to the state.
​
Proposition 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct financial and performance audits of the programs funded by any new tax measure, with results posted publicly. It also requires that all new taxes comply with the state's voter-approved spending limit - so that excess tax revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
If approved by voters, Prop 41 would require ongoing public audits to evaluate spending, identify waste, fraud or abuse, assess whether they are meeting their intended goals, and recommend improvements.
Learn More About Prop 41 (https://www.yesonprop41.org/about-prop41)
Endorsements
YES on Prop 41 is supported by a growing coalition of small businesses, taxpayers, good government advocates, elected officials, accountants and auditing experts.
Prop 41 is also supported by more than a million Californians who helped qualify the measure for the ballot.
Our Coalition (https://www.yesonprop41.org/)
"California families pay billions in state taxes every year and they deserve to see where that money goes and what it delivers. Proposition 41 brings real accountability and clear metrics to state spending. We're proud to support it."
Tracy Hernandez, Co-Founder and CEO of the New California Coalition
"This commonsense, long overdue reform will finally instill some transparency and accountability in state spending - ensuring Californians get better government services for the taxes we pay. It provides an independent, public report card for government spending, so government programs work better for everyone."
​
Pat Fong Kushida, President/CEO of the CalAsian Chamber
"Californians are paying more for everything, including some of the highest taxes in the country. Now more than ever, Californians deserve some relief from our state's high taxes. Prop 41 delivers."
​
Steve Westly, former Controller of California
California can't afford to keep funding programs with no accountability.
Current and former public auditors and a growing list of California residents and transparency advocates support Prop 41. Add your name to the list and join us in promoting greater accountability and better results.

Prop

CA
Prop
41
|
Constitutional Amendment
Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues From State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes.
Requires audits of citizen initiatives for special taxes. Imposes spending limits on all new special taxes.
SPUR's Recommendation
More transparency and accountability in government spending are worthy objectives. However, the Legislative Analyst’s Office and the state auditor already have the authority to evaluate policies and programs to ensure they are equitable and efficient. Prop. 41 was primarily placed on the ballot to defeat Prop. 40, a measure to tax billionaires. In addition, it would constrain local and state governments’ ability to raise revenue now and in the future for much-needed housing, transportation, infrastructure, and social services, which are already facing cuts at the federal and state levels.
Vote NO
What Prop. 41 Would Do
Proposition 41 would require the state auditor, working with the Legislative Analyst’s Office, to conduct an independent review of any state-level citizen initiative that aims to create a new special tax once it reaches 25% of the required signature threshold to be placed on the ballot. (Special taxes differ from general taxes in that they dedicate revenue to a specific purpose.) All new state-level special taxes would be audited every four years.
Additionally, any new special taxes passed after January 1, 2026 — whether proposed through legislation or through voter initiatives — would be subject to the Gann Limit, a voter-imposed revenue spending limit explained in the Backstory section below.
The audit of proposed citizen initiatives would examine the individual programs that would receive funding through the special tax and assess whether the programs are sufficiently cost-efficient in their hiring and operating practices. It would recommend how the programs could save 10% of their costs. The audit information would be included in the voter information guide, which would increase printing and mailing costs by a few hundred thousand dollars per initiative, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
If a special tax passes, the state auditor would be required to conduct audits every four years to assess spending, evaluate efficiency, and recommend improvements. The auditor would consider public input when measuring the program’s effectiveness. The revenues generated would cover implementation costs. However, the state would pay the initial audit cost if voters rejected the special tax.
Prop. 41 is a countermeasure to the so-called billionaire tax, Prop. 40 (https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/ca-prop-40-billionaire-tax). If both measures pass, the one receiving more votes would prevail.
The Backstory
Special taxes are taxes whose revenues are dedicated to a specific purpose rather than contributing to the state’s general fund budget. The State Legislature can levy special taxes with two-thirds voter approval, or an initiative placed on the ballot by voter signatures can do so with a simple majority (50% plus one vote). Currently, special taxes have no audit requirements or spending caps.
Since the late 1970s, California has faced numerous tax limitations through Prop. 13 and other constitutional amendments. The Gann Limit imposes requirements on how the state can spend General Fund revenues. If the state’s revenues exceed the Gann Limit — a dollar amount based on the state’s spending level in 1978–1979, adjusted for population and per capita income — half of revenues over the limit must be allocated to K–14 education and the other half returned to taxpayers. 1 Historically, the Gann Limit has rarely affected distribution of the state’s revenues, but if the state experiences strong income gains (including business/corporate/stock gains) over the limit, it could result in decreasing investment in state priorities such as housing, health care, economic development, and infrastructure.
The fiscal impacts of Prop. 41 are unknown. Adding pages to the voter information guide would cost money, but the audits could also create savings. If this measure prevents the state from raising new revenues from future taxes, it could have a significant negative fiscal impact in the longer term.
Prop. 41 is a countermeasure to Prop. 40, a one-time special tax on individuals with more than $1 billion in assets. Prop. 40 is intended to offset federal funding cuts to critical social safety net programs, including Medi-Cal, CalFresh, and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. The revenues generated from Prop. 40 would be exempt from the Gann Limit.
Prop. 41 was placed on the ballot through a signature-gathering effort led by Building a Better California, which is funded by Google co-founder Sergey Brin and other billionaires. It requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass. If it passes with more votes than Prop. 40, it would nullify Prop. 40. (Building a Better California has also placed Prop. 42 (https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/ca-prop-42-personal-property-taxes), a separate countermeasure to Prop. 40, on the ballot.)
Equity Impacts
Restricting spending from special taxes could negatively affect efforts to fund health care, food assistance, and other programs that disproportionately benefit lower-income Californians and communities of color.
Pro
Audits of proposed citizen initiatives could help ensure that the programs they would fund are cost-effective.
Cons
Prop. 41 was placed on the ballot to prevent a competing measure from succeeding. It could affect the state’s ability to raise revenue from other tax measures in the future.
Applying spending limits to new revenue measures could constrain local and state governments’ ability to fund urgent priorities amid unprecedented federal and state budget cuts.

Proposition 41: Audits For New State Special Taxes
Proposition 41: Audits For New State Special Taxes
Proposition 41: Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues From State Spending Limit. Requires Audits For New State Special Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Tax Audits, One-Time Wealth Tax for State-Funded Health Care Programs Initiative.
Improving Transparency, Effectiveness, and Efficiency in California Government Act of 2026
The Transparency Act
Summary
Proposition 41 was placed on the ballot by petition signatures to amend the California Constitution. It began as Initiative #25-0041A (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0040A1%20%28Gov.%20Efficiency%29.pdf) , filed with the California Attorney General’s Office. Prop. 41 amends the California Constitution by adding Article XXIV, creating audit review requirements for special tax measures and enforcing state appropriation limits (the Gann Limit) for all future state tax measures.
Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to conduct a financial and performance audit of any citizen initiative proposing a new special tax once the campaign collects 25% of required signatures. The auditor must review specific criteria set by Proposition 41, including identifying ways to cut the proposed program’s annual costs by 10%. If the measure qualifies, an executive summary of the audit is published in the official voter information pamphlet.
Additionally, the State Auditor will conduct ongoing audits every four years for programs receiving funding from special taxes created or increased by the Legislature or voters after January 1, 2026.
Proposition 41 specifies that the costs of these audits will be reimbursed using revenue generated from the new tax if voters approve the measure. If a special tax initiative fails, the state general fund covers the audit costs.
It would also prohibit the state from enforcing any new tax enacted or effective on or after January 1, 2026, that is exempted or excluded from the state spending limit.
Proposition 41 conflicts directly with Proposition 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/index.htm) (the Billionaire Wealth Tax initiative). If both pass, whichever measure receives more "yes" votes will prevail in its entirety. Because Proposition 40 excludes its revenues from the state spending limit, Proposition 41 would render Proposition 40 unenforceable if Proposition 41 wins more votes.
Note about the Gann Limit: Approved by California voters in 1979 asProposition 4 (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/ca_ballot_props/864/), the Gann Limit restricts how much tax revenue state and local governments (including school districts) can spend each year, adjusted annually for population changes and economic growth. The limit applies to both General Fund taxes (unrestricted funds for general government operations) and special taxes (funds earmarked for specific purposes), though certain spending categories—such as infrastructure and emergency response—are exempt. (Sources: California Budget Center, What is the Gann Limit? (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians) , Gann Limit (Wikipedia) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gann_Limit) , CA Department of Finance, Description of (https://dof.ca.gov/media/docs/budget/california-budget-frequently-asked-questions/fundclassifications.pdf)Fund Classifications in the Treasury (https://dof.ca.gov/media/docs/budget/california-budget-frequently-asked-questions/fundclassifications.pdf))
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
The net fiscal effect of Proposition 41 is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers. However, the State Auditor costs will increase due to the new and ongoing work to carry out the audit requirements in this measure.
Due to additional pages of audit information being included in the voter information guides could increase state printing and mailing costs by a few hundred thousand dollars per qualified initiative on the ballot.
What your vote means (LAO Analysis)
YES: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
NO: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that Proposition 41 improves transparency and reduces government waste by requiring independent state audits of programs funded by new special taxes while ensuring all state taxes respect voter-approved spending caps, as detailed in the Official Voter Information Guide.
Opponents contend that the measure was put on the ballot by billionaire opponents to block Prop. 40, a proposed wealth tax on billionaires, and that its audit requirements create unnecessary hurdles to funding essential public services like healthcare and education.

​ Yes on Proposition 41: Audits and Accountability for California Tax Dollars.
​
Billions of our tax dollars have flowed into state programs like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it. Californians deserve better education, healthcare, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned money we pay to the state.
​
Proposition 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct financial and performance audits of the programs funded by any new tax measure, with results posted publicly. It also requires that all new taxes comply with the state's voter-approved spending limit - so that excess tax revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
If approved by voters, Prop 41 would require ongoing public audits to evaluate spending, identify waste, fraud or abuse, assess whether they are meeting their intended goals, and recommend improvements.
Learn More About Prop 41 (https://www.yesonprop41.org/about-prop41)
Endorsements
YES on Prop 41 is supported by a growing coalition of small businesses, taxpayers, good government advocates, elected officials, accountants and auditing experts.
Prop 41 is also supported by more than a million Californians who helped qualify the measure for the ballot.
Our Coalition (https://www.yesonprop41.org/)
"California families pay billions in state taxes every year and they deserve to see where that money goes and what it delivers. Proposition 41 brings real accountability and clear metrics to state spending. We're proud to support it."
Tracy Hernandez, Co-Founder and CEO of the New California Coalition
"This commonsense, long overdue reform will finally instill some transparency and accountability in state spending - ensuring Californians get better government services for the taxes we pay. It provides an independent, public report card for government spending, so government programs work better for everyone."
​
Pat Fong Kushida, President/CEO of the CalAsian Chamber
"Californians are paying more for everything, including some of the highest taxes in the country. Now more than ever, Californians deserve some relief from our state's high taxes. Prop 41 delivers."
​
Steve Westly, former Controller of California
California can't afford to keep funding programs with no accountability.

Prop 40, The California Billionaire Tax
Proposition 40 is a one-time, 5% tax on billionaires. It demands that the ultra-wealthy pay their fair share to help protect healthcare for all Californians.
Trump slashed healthcare funding to give tax breaks to the richest Americans. The impacts: skyrocketing health insurance premiums, 3.4 million Californians losing health coverage, and clinics, ERs, and hospitals closing their doors.
Prop 40 restores this lost funding, stopping cost increases and ensuring Californians can get the care we need.
Billionaires like Sergey Brin and Peter Thiel are spending tens of millions in non-stop ads attacking Prop 40. They think they can fool us into voting no. But millions of Californians are about to prove them wrong.
Vote YES to finally tax billionaires.

How Prop 40 Will Help California.
Proposition 40 is a one-time, 5% tax only on Californians worth more than $1 billion—around 200 of the wealthiest people in the world. The other 39 million Californians will pay nothing.

The Crisis is Here.
We’re paying more because billionaires insist on paying less.

Healthcare costs keep rising—for all of us.
Read more
Working Californians are already struggling with the steep costs of healthcare. Trump’s federal funding cuts are pushing our premiums even higher. Up to 3.4 million Californians (https://ahea.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-01/ca-budget-and-policy-center-impact-of-federal-funding-cuts-2-pager.pdf) will lose access to coverage altogether.
Healthcare facilities are already closing.

Massive federal cuts have caused 7 clinics in Los Angeles County (http://publichealth.lacounty.gov/phcommon/public/media/mediapubhpdetail.cfm?prid=5253) to shut their doors. Another 83 hospitals and clinics (https://www.citizen.org/article/big-ugly-threat/) in California are at-risk of closing. It will be harder for all of us to get care when we need it.
How Prop 40 Helps California.
Protects access and limits price increases.
Read more
Allows 3.4 million Californian (https://ahea.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-01/ca-budget-and-policy-center-impact-of-federal-funding-cuts-2-pager.pdf)s to keep their health insurance and millions more not see their premiums skyrocket.
Keeps local hospitals and ERs open.
Read more
Restores lost federal funds that hospitals, clinics, nursing homes, and home care services rely on, ensuring millions of children, seniors, veterans, and families can access care.
Funds public schools and food assistance.
Read more
Prevents teacher layoffs in public schools and keeps kids and families fed through food assistance programs.

Proposition 41
Require audits of new tax programs
This proposition would make it harder to pass new special taxes by requiring the state auditor to review any special tax proposal before it goes to voters. The auditor would assess whether the program that would receive funding could cut spending by at least 10% annually. Any new special tax approved by voters would count toward California’s spending limit, potentially triggering automatic refunds that reduce funding for other state programs. If this proposition receives more votes than Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) (a wealth tax on billionaires), Proposition 40 is nullified, even if Proposition 40 also passes. It was placed on the ballot by opponents of the proposed billionaire tax.
Weigh the arguments.
Take our quizzes to learn more about each proposition.
BEGIN → (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/propositions/quizzes)

Summary
Support
Supporters say key social programs are not getting enough funding despite California’s high taxes. They argue the state auditor should assess whether the programs that would benefit from special taxes are spending money wisely. Supporters also want these special taxes to count toward the state spending limit, making tax rebates to Californians more likely.
Oppose
The chief opponent is SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, the sponsor of Proposition 40. The union argues that Prop. 41 is designed to trick voters into unknowingly blocking a wealth tax on billionaires. Prop. 41 isn’t about auditing waste in public programs, the union says; instead it’s a way for billionaires to avoid paying taxes once on their huge wealth.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Outside spending
Separate from proposition committees, outside groups can pay for ads, mailers and other efforts to influence voters. They can’t coordinate that spending with proposition committees. There is no limit on how much they can spend.

Frequently Asked Questions About Proposition 41
Q: What does Prop 41 do?
A: Prop 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct public performance and financial audits of programs funded by proposed new taxes, bringing government transparency and accountability to spending decisions before voters make them.
Californians pay some of the highest taxes in the country - on top of our high cost of living. Billions of our tax dollars have flowed into state programs, like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it. We deserve better education, healthcare, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned money we pay to the state.
Proposition 41 (2026) puts independent audits and measurable outcomes at the center of how California funds programs with new tax dollars, so that we stop funding failure and start funding successful outcomes.
Q: Does Prop 41 raise taxes?
A: No. Prop 41 does not create or increase any taxes - it protects taxpayers' interests by:
1) Identifying shortcomings in programs and recommending fixes, to help deliver better results for our taxes;
Reducing the waste and fraud that have cost California taxpayers billions of dollars in recent years; and
Requires all taxes to comply with the state's voter-approved spending limit - including its requirement that excess revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
Prop 41 ensures taxpayers get better results, not just a bigger tax bill.
Q: How do the audits work?
Proposition 41 requires the independent California State Auditor to review programs that would be funded by a new or higher special tax proposed to California voters. The first review happens before the tax reaches the ballot. Once a special tax initiative collects 25 percent of the signatures needed to qualify, the State Auditor audits each program that would receive the money, looking at whether the program is achieving its goals, how well it spends its dollars, and where fraud, waste, or abuse may exist. A summary of the findings is printed in the Voter Information Guide so voters can read it before they vote. If a new special tax is approved by voters, the State Auditor reviews the funded programs again every four years and invites public input.
The audits produce findings and recommendations, and both are public. Decisions about funding stay with voters and the Legislature, as they are today, and the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst Office notes that acting on the recommendations "could result in savings or improved
services at existing funding levels." A program funded by a new special tax is reviewed before any change to its funding is made. For a full walkthrough, see the our explainer here (https://www.yesonprop41.org/how-audits-work) .
Q: Who conducts the audits?
A: The audits are conducted by California's independent State Auditor, the state's nonpartisan fiscal watchdog, and shared broadly with the public, including in the Voter Information Guide. The financial and performance audits must:
Track all program spending and assess whether it's achieving its intended outcomes;
Determine whether programs have sufficient oversight and accountability;
Identify areas of waste, fraud and abuse; and,
Recommend how future waste and fraud can be avoided and how programs can be made more effective.
Under Prop 41, the Auditor is required to review programs funded by proposed new tax measures before voters cast their ballots and conduct ongoing audits if those measures are approved.
Q: What happens if an audit finds problems?
A: If the State Auditor identifies concerns about oversight, accountability or program performance, those findings are included in the Voter Information Guide so voters can make a more informed decision.
If a measure is approved, future audits continue evaluating how funds are spent, identify areas for improvement, and recommend ways to make programs more effective over time - so that programs are held accountable to the people who pay for them: taxpayers.
The audit doesn't decide whether a measure passes or fails; it gives voters independent information before they cast their ballot.
Q: What does Prop 41 mean for education, healthcare and other public programs?
A: Every tax dollar we waste is a dollar that could actually help someone. Prop 41 is built to sustain fiscal discipline alongside public investment. It does not cut or eliminate funding for education, healthcare or other public services, and it helps ensure that programs funded by taxpayers are transparent, accountable and delivering results. We deserve better services in return for the hard-earned money we pay to the state.
Prop 41 requires more accountability, transparency and trackable progress of programs funded by our taxes, like homelessness (https://www.yesonprop41.org/homelessness) , so that we stop funding failure and start funding successful outcomes.
Q: Does Prop 41 make it harder for initiatives to qualify for the ballot?
A: No. Prop 41 does not change the initiative process or prevent measures from qualifying for the ballot. Supporters can still gather signatures, qualify initiatives and campaign for their proposals just as they do today.
The difference is that under Prop 41, programs to be funded by new taxes are assessed before voters cast their ballot. The Auditor's findings must be posted in the Voter Information Guide, so voters have access to independent information about how programs are being managed and whether they actually need more funding. Voters deserve the ability to make informed decisions about new taxes without having to rely on information from special interests or politicians.
Q: Who pays for the audits?
A: If a tax measure is approved, the cost of the required audits is paid from the revenues generated by that measure. If voters reject the measure, the audit costs are paid through the state's General Fund.
Many statewide tax measures raise hundreds of millions - or even billions - of dollars over time. Prop 41 ensures a small investment in independent oversight helps taxpayers know whether those dollars are being spent effectively and producing the results promised.
Q: Who supports Prop 41?
Prop 41 is backed by a board coalition of small businesses, taxpayers, good government advocates, accountants, and auditing experts. Endorsers include the California Society of Certified Public Accountants, former State Controller Steve Westly, former California Auditor General Tom Hayes, the NAACP California-Hawaii State Conference, the California Alliance of Seniors, the California Chamber of Commerce, the California Farm Bureau, the California Taxpayers Association, the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, along with dozens of local chambers, taxpayer associations, and regional economic partnerships across the state.
Endorsements also include Democratic organizations and officials. The Chinese American Democratic Club, the San Bernardino Young Democrats, and the Sacramento State College Democrats have endorsed Prop 41, as has Steve Westly, a Democrat who served as State Controller. Local officials who have endorsed include Riverside County Auditor-Controller Ben Benoit and council members and mayors from across California. The full and current list of endorsers is at yesonprop41.org/endorsements (https://www.yesonprop41.org/endorsements) .
Q: How does Prop 41 strengthen taxpayer protections?
A: Prop 41 requires all future state tax measures to comply with California's voter-approved constitutional spending limit. That means future measures must follow the same constitutional rules that already apply to state spending including the requirement that excess revenues be refunded to taxpayers when the spending limit is exceeded.
Prop 41 provides for consistent application of the spending limit, so future state tax measures follow the same constitutional rules that already govern state spending, including the requirement that excess revenues be refunded to taxpayers.

What Would Proposition 41 Mean for California?
Understanding the Proposed Audit Requirements for Special Taxes and the Prohibition on Excluding Revenues from the State Spending Limit
September 2026 | By Kayla Kitson (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/kayla-kitson/)
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Prop. 41 would 1) impose new audit requirements for programs funded with state special taxes and 2) prohibit the collection of new state taxes that are excluded from the state’s spending limit. The primary intent of the measure is to invalidate Prop. 40 — the billionaire tax also appearing on the November ballot — but Prop. 41 could also make it harder for the state to meet the needs of Californians in the future.
What Would Prop. 41 Do?
Prop. 41 would amend the state Constitution to impose new rules related to state taxes. The measure would require “financial and performance audits” of programs receiving revenues from special taxes and would also prevent state taxes from being excluded from California’s spending cap, also known as the “Gann Limit.”
Creates New Audit Requirements for Special Taxes
Prop. 41 would create new pre-election and ongoing audit requirements for programs receiving — or proposed to receive — revenues from state-level special taxes. In contrast to a general tax, which can be used for any purpose, a special tax raises revenue for specific purposes.
Pre-election audits: The State Auditor would be required to perform an audit of any program that would be funded by a special tax proposed through a statewide voter initiative. The audit would be required while the initiative is being circulated for signatures — before it officially qualifies for the ballot — and a summary of the audit findings would be included in the voter information guide. The full audit would also be made available to the public.
Ongoing audits: The State Auditor would be required to audit programs receiving revenues from special taxes enacted by the Legislature or approved by voters through a statewide initiative on or after January 1, 2026. These audits would be required every four years.
The audits would assess programs based on specific criteria outlined in Prop. 41, and would require the State Auditor to recommend how programs could reduce costs by at least 10% annually.
The State Auditor would be reimbursed for the costs of these audits with revenues from the relevant special tax. If, however, a special tax initiative fails to qualify for the ballot or is rejected by voters, the audit costs would be absorbed by the state’s General Fund.
Prohibits Taxes That Are Excluded from the State Spending Limit
Prop. 41 would prevent the state from collecting or enforcing any state tax that is 1) enacted on or after January 1, 2026 and 2) excluded from the state spending cap, also known as the Gann Limit (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians/). Currently, the measure would apply only to Prop. 40 if both measures pass and Prop. 41 receives more votes, but it could potentially be applied to other tax policy proposals in the future.
California’s spending limit was established by Prop. 4 (1979) and is based on state spending in 1978-79, annually adjusted for population changes and inflation. Under the state Constitution, if state revenues exceed the limit over two consecutive years, the excess must be split equally between refunds to taxpayers and spending on TK-14 education. In effect, the spending limit restricts the ability of state leaders to raise and spend revenue to meet the most pressing needs of Californians.
Conflicts with Other Measures on the Ballot
The California Constitution states that if provisions of multiple measures on the same ballot conflict, the provisions of the measure receiving the higher number of votes will prevail. Prop. 41 broadly specifies that if another measure on the same ballot either 1) imposes different audit rules on special taxes or 2) contains a tax that is exempted from the state spending limit, the entirety of the other measure would be invalidated if Prop. 41 receives more votes.
Prop. 41 is in direct conflict with Prop. 40. (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/) This is because Prop. 40 would create a one-time tax on the wealth of billionaires and exclude the revenues from the state spending limit, which Prop. 41 prohibits.
If both measures were to be approved and Prop. 41 received more votes, Prop. 40 could be invalidated. Alternatively, if both measures pass but Prop. 40 receives more votes, the billionaire tax could be collected, but it is possible that audits would be required of Medi-Cal and other programs receiving Prop. 40 dollars. If both measures pass, there may be litigation regarding the application of conflicting provisions, and the final decision would be made by the courts.
How Would Prop. 41 Affect Californians and the State Budget?
The primary intent of Prop. 41 is to invalidate the Prop. 40 billionaire tax, but it would also create new barriers to raising state revenue and effectively meeting the needs of Californians.
Prop. 41 would also increase state costs related to conducting audits for programs that are often already subject to close scrutiny — reducing funding available to support critical state services. This would come at a time when Californians are already dealing with affordability concerns as well as the consequences of the steep federal cuts to health care and food assistance enacted in H.R. 1 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/timeline-of-funding-cuts-to-medi-cal-and-calfresh-in-california/), signed by President Trump in 2025.
Impacts of Audit Requirements
The pre-election audit requirement could dissuade voters from approving special tax initiatives that would raise needed revenue to support and improve state services that help Californians stay healthy, housed, and economically secure. A summary of the audit would appear in the voter guide, and voters could interpret it as evidence that the programs to be funded are inefficient or ineffective. For example, because the State Auditor would be required to recommend options to cut program costs by 10%, voters may assume this means the program is inefficient even if that is not the case.
Additionally, the requirement for cost-cutting recommendations could result in service cuts with real human impacts. While policymakers would be under no obligation to implement these recommendations, if they did it could result in cuts to core services rather than simply “inefficient spending.” For example, if a program receiving special tax revenues is already operating efficiently but the Auditor must identify ways that costs could be reduced by 10%, lawmakers may be under pressure to adopt those recommendations — particularly in difficult budget times. Those cuts could lead to fewer Californians being served, reductions in benefit levels, or decreased service quality.
While it is clearly important for tax dollars to be spent efficiently and effectively, many state programs are already subject to occasional or ongoing audits. The State Auditor currently performs audits as a result of (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/about-us/#where-our-work-comes-from) existing state laws, legislative requests, and whistleblower tips. Additionally, the “High-Risk” audit program requires the Auditor to periodically review programs or agencies determined to be at high risk for “waste, fraud, abuse, or mismanagement” or those raising concerns related to efficiency or effectiveness.
Prop. 41’s additional audits would increase state costs, reducing the resources available to directly support services for Californians. Moreover, in the case of program audits related to a proposed special tax, the audit costs would be absorbed by the state’s General Fund if the ballot initiative were not enacted, leaving less funding for critical state services like education, health care, and human services.
Impacts of State Spending Limit Provisions
The primary impact of preventing new revenues from being excluded from the spending limit would be the invalidation of the billionaire tax proposed by Prop. 40 — if both measures pass and Prop. 41 receives more votes.
In the future, voters may be able to exclude the revenues from a statewide tax initiative from the spending cap if the initiative amends the Constitution to do so. In fact, previous initiatives have explicitly excluded new tax revenues from the limit, such as tobacco taxes enacted under Prop. 10 (1998) and Prop. 56 (2016). However, legal challenges are possible and there is no certainty on how courts would rule.
State policymakers already lack the authority to exclude new tax revenues from the spending cap without voter approval because the cap is enshrined in the state Constitution.
There are some existing state revenue streams that could potentially be affected by Prop. 41, but there are many complications and uncertainties and any conflicts would ultimately be decided by the courts. For example, some health care financing sources that must be occasionally reauthorized — such as the Managed Care Organization (MCO) tax and the Hospital Quality Assurance fee, which both allow the state to draw down additional federal funding for Medi-Cal — could potentially be impacted by Prop. 41. This, in turn, would jeopardize billions of dollars in federal funding for Medi-Cal at a time when Californians are already experiencing the harms of the deep federal cuts to health care resulting from H.R. 1.
Who Supports and Opposes Prop. 41?
The top contributor to the Prop. 41 campaign is a group called “Building a Better California,” which is largely funded (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1486767&view=received) by Google cofounder Sergey Brin and other billionaires. This same group is also opposing Prop. 40 and supporting Prop. 42. Prop. 41 is also endorsed by the California Republican Party, the California Chamber of Commerce, and the California Taxpayers Association.
There is no official campaign against Prop. 41. However, prominent opponents include the Service Employees International Union – United Health Workers West (SEIU–UHW) — the main proponent of the Prop. 40 billionaire tax measure — as well as other labor groups including the California Federation of Teachers and the California Federation of Labor Unions. The California Democratic Party and the League of Women Voters also oppose Prop. 41.

Real Problems, Real Solutions
California voters have approved nearly $200 billion in special taxes, bonds, and dedicated revenue over the last two decades. A review of these revenue measures finds a persistent pattern of hoarded funds, missing outcome data, broken promises, and ballooning costs across nearly every major initiative. Prop 41 requires trackable progress of programs funded by our taxes, which includes audits both before taxes are voted on by voters, and ongoing audits of programs funded by taxes if they are approved.

The Common Thread
None of these failures happened because Californians were unwilling to invest in solving hard problems. They happened because money went out the door without a clear, public accounting of whether it was working. Prop 41 answers that gap directly. Before voters approve a new special tax, they see an independent audit of the programs it would fund, including concrete recommendations for savings and improvement. After approval, those programs face recurring audits that keep the accounting honest. Californians get trackable progress, real results, and confidence that their tax dollars are delivering for the people these programs are meant to serve.
At a time when Californians are paying some of the highest taxes in the nation and facing rising everyday costs, voters deserve confidence that their tax dollars are being spent efficiently. When we have transparency and accountability, our tax dollars are better spent providing the services and programs Californians need.

Proposition 41
Require audits of new tax programs
This proposition would make it harder to pass new special taxes by requiring the state auditor to review any special tax proposal before it goes to voters. The auditor would assess whether the program that would receive funding could cut spending by at least 10% annually. Any new special tax approved by voters would count toward California’s spending limit, potentially triggering automatic refunds that reduce funding for other state programs. If this proposition receives more votes than Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) (a wealth tax on billionaires), Proposition 40 is nullified, even if Proposition 40 also passes. It was placed on the ballot by opponents of the proposed billionaire tax.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Proposition 41
Require audits of new tax programs
This proposition would make it harder to pass new special taxes by requiring the state auditor to review any special tax proposal before it goes to voters. The auditor would assess whether the program that would receive funding could cut spending by at least 10% annually. Any new special tax approved by voters would count toward California’s spending limit, potentially triggering automatic refunds that reduce funding for other state programs. If this proposition receives more votes than Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) (a wealth tax on billionaires), Proposition 40 is nullified, even if Proposition 40 also passes. It was placed on the ballot by opponents of the proposed billionaire tax.

Supporters say key social programs are not getting enough funding despite California’s high taxes. They argue the state auditor should assess whether the programs that would benefit from special taxes are spending money wisely. Supporters also want these special taxes to count toward the state spending limit, making tax rebates to Californians more likely.
Oppose
The chief opponent is SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, the sponsor of Proposition 40. The union argues that Prop. 41 is designed to trick voters into unknowingly blocking a wealth tax on billionaires. Prop. 41 isn’t about auditing waste in public programs, the union says; instead it’s a way for billionaires to avoid paying taxes once on their huge wealth.

What Would Proposition 41 Mean for California?
Understanding the Proposed Audit Requirements for Special Taxes and the Prohibition on Excluding Revenues from the State Spending Limit
September 2026 | By Kayla Kitson (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/kayla-kitson/)
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Prop. 41 would 1) impose new audit requirements for programs funded with state special taxes and 2) prohibit the collection of new state taxes that are excluded from the state’s spending limit. The primary intent of the measure is to invalidate Prop. 40 — the billionaire tax also appearing on the November ballot — but Prop. 41 could also make it harder for the state to meet the needs of Californians in the future.
What Would Prop. 41 Do?
Prop. 41 would amend the state Constitution to impose new rules related to state taxes. The measure would require “financial and performance audits” of programs receiving revenues from special taxes and would also prevent state taxes from being excluded from California’s spending cap, also known as the “Gann Limit.”
Creates New Audit Requirements for Special Taxes
Prop. 41 would create new pre-election and ongoing audit requirements for programs receiving — or proposed to receive — revenues from state-level special taxes. In contrast to a general tax, which can be used for any purpose, a special tax raises revenue for specific purposes.
Pre-election audits: The State Auditor would be required to perform an audit of any program that would be funded by a special tax proposed through a statewide voter initiative. The audit would be required while the initiative is being circulated for signatures — before it officially qualifies for the ballot — and a summary of the audit findings would be included in the voter information guide. The full audit would also be made available to the public.
Ongoing audits: The State Auditor would be required to audit programs receiving revenues from special taxes enacted by the Legislature or approved by voters through a statewide initiative on or after January 1, 2026. These audits would be required every four years.
The audits would assess programs based on specific criteria outlined in Prop. 41, and would require the State Auditor to recommend how programs could reduce costs by at least 10% annually.
The State Auditor would be reimbursed for the costs of these audits with revenues from the relevant special tax. If, however, a special tax initiative fails to qualify for the ballot or is rejected by voters, the audit costs would be absorbed by the state’s General Fund.
Prohibits Taxes That Are Excluded from the State Spending Limit
Prop. 41 would prevent the state from collecting or enforcing any state tax that is 1) enacted on or after January 1, 2026 and 2) excluded from the state spending cap, also known as the Gann Limit (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians/). Currently, the measure would apply only to Prop. 40 if both measures pass and Prop. 41 receives more votes, but it could potentially be applied to other tax policy proposals in the future.
California’s spending limit was established by Prop. 4 (1979) and is based on state spending in 1978-79, annually adjusted for population changes and inflation. Under the state Constitution, if state revenues exceed the limit over two consecutive years, the excess must be split equally between refunds to taxpayers and spending on TK-14 education. In effect, the spending limit restricts the ability of state leaders to raise and spend revenue to meet the most pressing needs of Californians.
Conflicts with Other Measures on the Ballot
The California Constitution states that if provisions of multiple measures on the same ballot conflict, the provisions of the measure receiving the higher number of votes will prevail. Prop. 41 broadly specifies that if another measure on the same ballot either 1) imposes different audit rules on special taxes or 2) contains a tax that is exempted from the state spending limit, the entirety of the other measure would be invalidated if Prop. 41 receives more votes.
Prop. 41 is in direct conflict with Prop. 40. (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/) This is because Prop. 40 would create a one-time tax on the wealth of billionaires and exclude the revenues from the state spending limit, which Prop. 41 prohibits.
If both measures were to be approved and Prop. 41 received more votes, Prop. 40 could be invalidated. Alternatively, if both measures pass but Prop. 40 receives more votes, the billionaire tax could be collected, but it is possible that audits would be required of Medi-Cal and other programs receiving Prop. 40 dollars. If both measures pass, there may be litigation regarding the application of conflicting provisions, and the final decision would be made by the courts.
How Would Prop. 41 Affect Californians and the State Budget?
The primary intent of Prop. 41 is to invalidate the Prop. 40 billionaire tax, but it would also create new barriers to raising state revenue and effectively meeting the needs of Californians.
Prop. 41 would also increase state costs related to conducting audits for programs that are often already subject to close scrutiny — reducing funding available to support critical state services. This would come at a time when Californians are already dealing with affordability concerns as well as the consequences of the steep federal cuts to health care and food assistance enacted in H.R. 1 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/timeline-of-funding-cuts-to-medi-cal-and-calfresh-in-california/), signed by President Trump in 2025.
Impacts of Audit Requirements
The pre-election audit requirement could dissuade voters from approving special tax initiatives that would raise needed revenue to support and improve state services that help Californians stay healthy, housed, and economically secure. A summary of the audit would appear in the voter guide, and voters could interpret it as evidence that the programs to be funded are inefficient or ineffective. For example, because the State Auditor would be required to recommend options to cut program costs by 10%, voters may assume this means the program is inefficient even if that is not the case.
Additionally, the requirement for cost-cutting recommendations could result in service cuts with real human impacts. While policymakers would be under no obligation to implement these recommendations, if they did it could result in cuts to core services rather than simply “inefficient spending.” For example, if a program receiving special tax revenues is already operating efficiently but the Auditor must identify ways that costs could be reduced by 10%, lawmakers may be under pressure to adopt those recommendations — particularly in difficult budget times. Those cuts could lead to fewer Californians being served, reductions in benefit levels, or decreased service quality.
While it is clearly important for tax dollars to be spent efficiently and effectively, many state programs are already subject to occasional or ongoing audits. The State Auditor currently performs audits as a result of (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/about-us/#where-our-work-comes-from) existing state laws, legislative requests, and whistleblower tips. Additionally, the “High-Risk” audit program requires the Auditor to periodically review programs or agencies determined to be at high risk for “waste, fraud, abuse, or mismanagement” or those raising concerns related to efficiency or effectiveness.
Prop. 41’s additional audits would increase state costs, reducing the resources available to directly support services for Californians. Moreover, in the case of program audits related to a proposed special tax, the audit costs would be absorbed by the state’s General Fund if the ballot initiative were not enacted, leaving less funding for critical state services like education, health care, and human services.
Impacts of State Spending Limit Provisions
The primary impact of preventing new revenues from being excluded from the spending limit would be the invalidation of the billionaire tax proposed by Prop. 40 — if both measures pass and Prop. 41 receives more votes.
In the future, voters may be able to exclude the revenues from a statewide tax initiative from the spending cap if the initiative amends the Constitution to do so. In fact, previous initiatives have explicitly excluded new tax revenues from the limit, such as tobacco taxes enacted under Prop. 10 (1998) and Prop. 56 (2016). However, legal challenges are possible and there is no certainty on how courts would rule.
State policymakers already lack the authority to exclude new tax revenues from the spending cap without voter approval because the cap is enshrined in the state Constitution.
There are some existing state revenue streams that could potentially be affected by Prop. 41, but there are many complications and uncertainties and any conflicts would ultimately be decided by the courts. For example, some health care financing sources that must be occasionally reauthorized — such as the Managed Care Organization (MCO) tax and the Hospital Quality Assurance fee, which both allow the state to draw down additional federal funding for Medi-Cal — could potentially be impacted by Prop. 41. This, in turn, would jeopardize billions of dollars in federal funding for Medi-Cal at a time when Californians are already experiencing the harms of the deep federal cuts to health care resulting from H.R. 1.
Who Supports and Opposes Prop. 41?
The top contributor to the Prop. 41 campaign is a group called “Building a Better California,” which is largely funded (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1486767&view=received) by Google cofounder Sergey Brin and other billionaires. This same group is also opposing Prop. 40 and supporting Prop. 42. Prop. 41 is also endorsed by the California Republican Party, the California Chamber of Commerce, and the California Taxpayers Association.
There is no official campaign against Prop. 41. However, prominent opponents include the Service Employees International Union – United Health Workers West (SEIU–UHW) — the main proponent of the Prop. 40 billionaire tax measure — as well as other labor groups including the California Federation of Teachers and the California Federation of Labor Unions. The California Democratic Party and the League of Women Voters also oppose Prop. 41.

What Would Proposition 41 Mean for California?
Understanding the Proposed Audit Requirements for Special Taxes and the Prohibition on Excluding Revenues from the State Spending Limit
September 2026 | By Kayla Kitson (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/kayla-kitson/)
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Prop. 41 would 1) impose new audit requirements for programs funded with state special taxes and 2) prohibit the collection of new state taxes that are excluded from the state’s spending limit. The primary intent of the measure is to invalidate Prop. 40 — the billionaire tax also appearing on the November ballot — but Prop. 41 could also make it harder for the state to meet the needs of Californians in the future.
What Would Prop. 41 Do?
Prop. 41 would amend the state Constitution to impose new rules related to state taxes. The measure would require “financial and performance audits” of programs receiving revenues from special taxes and would also prevent state taxes from being excluded from California’s spending cap, also known as the “Gann Limit.”
Creates New Audit Requirements for Special Taxes
Prop. 41 would create new pre-election and ongoing audit requirements for programs receiving — or proposed to receive — revenues from state-level special taxes. In contrast to a general tax, which can be used for any purpose, a special tax raises revenue for specific purposes.
Pre-election audits: The State Auditor would be required to perform an audit of any program that would be funded by a special tax proposed through a statewide voter initiative. The audit would be required while the initiative is being circulated for signatures — before it officially qualifies for the ballot — and a summary of the audit findings would be included in the voter information guide. The full audit would also be made available to the public.
Ongoing audits: The State Auditor would be required to audit programs receiving revenues from special taxes enacted by the Legislature or approved by voters through a statewide initiative on or after January 1, 2026. These audits would be required every four years.
The audits would assess programs based on specific criteria outlined in Prop. 41, and would require the State Auditor to recommend how programs could reduce costs by at least 10% annually.
The State Auditor would be reimbursed for the costs of these audits with revenues from the relevant special tax. If, however, a special tax initiative fails to qualify for the ballot or is rejected by voters, the audit costs would be absorbed by the state’s General Fund.
Prohibits Taxes That Are Excluded from the State Spending Limit
Prop. 41 would prevent the state from collecting or enforcing any state tax that is 1) enacted on or after January 1, 2026 and 2) excluded from the state spending cap, also known as the Gann Limit (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians/). Currently, the measure would apply only to Prop. 40 if both measures pass and Prop. 41 receives more votes, but it could potentially be applied to other tax policy proposals in the future.
California’s spending limit was established by Prop. 4 (1979) and is based on state spending in 1978-79, annually adjusted for population changes and inflation. Under the state Constitution, if state revenues exceed the limit over two consecutive years, the excess must be split equally between refunds to taxpayers and spending on TK-14 education. In effect, the spending limit restricts the ability of state leaders to raise and spend revenue to meet the most pressing needs of Californians.
Conflicts with Other Measures on the Ballot
The California Constitution states that if provisions of multiple measures on the same ballot conflict, the provisions of the measure receiving the higher number of votes will prevail. Prop. 41 broadly specifies that if another measure on the same ballot either 1) imposes different audit rules on special taxes or 2) contains a tax that is exempted from the state spending limit, the entirety of the other measure would be invalidated if Prop. 41 receives more votes.
Prop. 41 is in direct conflict with Prop. 40. (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/) This is because Prop. 40 would create a one-time tax on the wealth of billionaires and exclude the revenues from the state spending limit, which Prop. 41 prohibits.
If both measures were to be approved and Prop. 41 received more votes, Prop. 40 could be invalidated. Alternatively, if both measures pass but Prop. 40 receives more votes, the billionaire tax could be collected, but it is possible that audits would be required of Medi-Cal and other programs receiving Prop. 40 dollars. If both measures pass, there may be litigation regarding the application of conflicting provisions, and the final decision would be made by the courts.
How Would Prop. 41 Affect Californians and the State Budget?
The primary intent of Prop. 41 is to invalidate the Prop. 40 billionaire tax, but it would also create new barriers to raising state revenue and effectively meeting the needs of Californians.
Prop. 41 would also increase state costs related to conducting audits for programs that are often already subject to close scrutiny — reducing funding available to support critical state services. This would come at a time when Californians are already dealing with affordability concerns as well as the consequences of the steep federal cuts to health care and food assistance enacted in H.R. 1 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/timeline-of-funding-cuts-to-medi-cal-and-calfresh-in-california/), signed by President Trump in 2025.
Impacts of Audit Requirements
The pre-election audit requirement could dissuade voters from approving special tax initiatives that would raise needed revenue to support and improve state services that help Californians stay healthy, housed, and economically secure. A summary of the audit would appear in the voter guide, and voters could interpret it as evidence that the programs to be funded are inefficient or ineffective. For example, because the State Auditor would be required to recommend options to cut program costs by 10%, voters may assume this means the program is inefficient even if that is not the case.
Additionally, the requirement for cost-cutting recommendations could result in service cuts with real human impacts. While policymakers would be under no obligation to implement these recommendations, if they did it could result in cuts to core services rather than simply “inefficient spending.” For example, if a program receiving special tax revenues is already operating efficiently but the Auditor must identify ways that costs could be reduced by 10%, lawmakers may be under pressure to adopt those recommendations — particularly in difficult budget times. Those cuts could lead to fewer Californians being served, reductions in benefit levels, or decreased service quality.
While it is clearly important for tax dollars to be spent efficiently and effectively, many state programs are already subject to occasional or ongoing audits. The State Auditor currently performs audits as a result of (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/about-us/#where-our-work-comes-from) existing state laws, legislative requests, and whistleblower tips. Additionally, the “High-Risk” audit program requires the Auditor to periodically review programs or agencies determined to be at high risk for “waste, fraud, abuse, or mismanagement” or those raising concerns related to efficiency or effectiveness.
Prop. 41’s additional audits would increase state costs, reducing the resources available to directly support services for Californians. Moreover, in the case of program audits related to a proposed special tax, the audit costs would be absorbed by the state’s General Fund if the ballot initiative were not enacted, leaving less funding for critical state services like education, health care, and human services.
Impacts of State Spending Limit Provisions
The primary impact of preventing new revenues from being excluded from the spending limit would be the invalidation of the billionaire tax proposed by Prop. 40 — if both measures pass and Prop. 41 receives more votes.
In the future, voters may be able to exclude the revenues from a statewide tax initiative from the spending cap if the initiative amends the Constitution to do so. In fact, previous initiatives have explicitly excluded new tax revenues from the limit, such as tobacco taxes enacted under Prop. 10 (1998) and Prop. 56 (2016). However, legal challenges are possible and there is no certainty on how courts would rule.
State policymakers already lack the authority to exclude new tax revenues from the spending cap without voter approval because the cap is enshrined in the state Constitution.
There are some existing state revenue streams that could potentially be affected by Prop. 41, but there are many complications and uncertainties and any conflicts would ultimately be decided by the courts. For example, some health care financing sources that must be occasionally reauthorized — such as the Managed Care Organization (MCO) tax and the Hospital Quality Assurance fee, which both allow the state to draw down additional federal funding for Medi-Cal — could potentially be impacted by Prop. 41. This, in turn, would jeopardize billions of dollars in federal funding for Medi-Cal at a time when Californians are already experiencing the harms of the deep federal cuts to health care resulting from H.R. 1.
Who Supports and Opposes Prop. 41?
The top contributor to the Prop. 41 campaign is a group called “Building a Better California,” which is largely funded (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1486767&view=received) by Google cofounder Sergey Brin and other billionaires. This same group is also opposing Prop. 40 and supporting Prop. 42. Prop. 41 is also endorsed by the California Republican Party, the California Chamber of Commerce, and the California Taxpayers Association.
There is no official campaign against Prop. 41. However, prominent opponents include the Service Employees International Union – United Health Workers West (SEIU–UHW) — the main proponent of the Prop. 40 billionaire tax measure — as well as other labor groups including the California Federation of Teachers and the California Federation of Labor Unions. The California Democratic Party and the League of Women Voters also oppose Prop. 41.
