Homelessness in California
The State Must Do More to Assess the Cost-Effectiveness of Its Homelessness Programs
Background
The Joint Legislative Audit Committee requested an audit of the State’s homelessness funding and an evaluation of the State’s efforts to
monitor the cost-effectiveness of such spending. This report (2023-102.1) focuses primarily on the State’s activities as carried out by the
California Interagency Council on Homelessness (Cal ICH). More than 180,000 Californians experienced homelessness in 2023—a 53 percent
increase from 2013. To address this ongoing crisis, nine state agencies have collectively spent billions of dollars in state funding over the past
five years administering at least 30 programs dedicated to preventing and ending homelessness. Cal ICH is responsible for coordinating,
developing, and evaluating the efforts of these nine agencies.
Our Key Recommendations
• The Legislature should amend state law to require
Cal ICH, by March 2025, to mandate reporting by
state agencies of costs and outcomes of state-funded
homelessness programs. To implement such reporting,
the Legislature should require Cal ICH to develop
guidance establishing specifics on uniformity of data
to be collected and how it is to be presented. The
Legislature should require Cal ICH to annually compile
and report this cost and outcome information publicly
beginning in September 2025 and should provide
resources for this effort, as necessary.
• Cal ICH should request that state agencies responsible
for administering state-funded homelessness programs
provide spending- and outcome-related information for
people entering, experiencing, and exiting homelessness.
By March 2025, Cal ICH should develop and publish on
its website a scorecard—or similar instrument—that
would give the Legislature and other policymakers
the information necessary to better understand each
homelessness program’s specific costs and outcomes.
Cal ICH should determine and request from the
Legislature any necessary resources required for this effort.
Key Findings
• Cal ICH has not consistently tracked and evaluated the State’s efforts to
end homelessness.
» Because Cal ICH has not tracked and reported on the State’s funding
for homelessness programs since its 2023 assessment covering fiscal
years 2018–19 through 2020–21, the State and its policymakers are
likely to struggle to understand homelessness programs’ ongoing costs
and achieved outcomes.
» Cal ICH has not established a consistent method for gathering
information on homelessness programs’ costs and outcomes, leaving
the State without information that would allow decision-makers to
make data-driven decisions.
• Two of the five state-funded programs we reviewed are likely cost-effective.
» Homekey allows the State to provide individuals with housing that is
less expensive than newly built affordable housing units. The Housing
Support Program helps house families who are at risk of or experiencing
homelessness and costs less than the State would spend if these
families were homeless.
» The Encampment Resolution Funding program; the Homeless Housing,
Assistance and Prevention program; and the State Rental Assistance
Program did not collect adequate data on program outcomes to assess
their cost-effectiveness.

PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Nullifies state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that exempt their revenues from voter-approved state spending limit. Requires pre-election and recurring audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Fiscal Impact: The net fiscal effect is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers. Supporters: CA Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian Chamber of Commerce; California Taxpayers Association (CalTax) Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Californians deserve better results for our taxes. Billions have flowed into programs like homelessness, with too little to show for it. Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct PUBLIC AUDITS of programs funded by new taxes—so we get more transparency, more accountability and better outcomes for taxpayers.
CON
Prop. 41 isn’t really about audits—it’s a billionaire-funded trick designed to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Vote NO on 41.

PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Elections Administration. The Secretary of State oversees elections across the state and prepares and mails the state Voter Information Guide (VIG).
Voter Initiative Process. California citizens may propose state laws and constitutional amendments through the statewide initiative process. Supporters of an initiative collect signatures from registered voters to qualify their initiative for the ballot. State law sets how many valid signatures supporters must collect to qualify their initiative for the ballot. Supporters notify the Secretary of State once they have gathered 25 percent of the necessary signatures.
Special Taxes. State taxes can be raised by the Legislature or by voters. When a “special tax” is created, the revenue from that tax is dedicated to a specific purpose or program. For example, certain fuel taxes can only be used to pay for public roads and other transportation programs.
California State Auditor’s Office (State Auditor). The State Auditor is an independent and nonpartisan office in state government. It reviews how well the state and local governments follow the law, use money, and run their programs. These reviews are called audits. An audit may give recommendations to help improve government operations and efficiency. Some audits happen regularly over time while other audits are done only once.
PROPOSAL
Requires One-Time Audits Before Special Taxes Appear on the Ballot Through the Voter Initiative Process. Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to review each program that would receive funds from a new or increased special tax proposed through the voter initiative process. This audit would occur after supporters collect 25 percent of the signatures needed to qualify a measure for the ballot, which is before it is known whether the initiative will qualify for the ballot. Proposition 41 specifies what the State Auditor would include in these audits, including identifying ways to reduce an audited program’s annual costs by 10 percent. Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to write a summary of each audit. If a proposed voter initiative with a special tax qualifies for the ballot, Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor’s summary to be included in the VIG. If voters approve the special tax, the cost of the one-time audit would be paid from the new tax revenues.
Ongoing Audits of Programs Receiving Funds From New or Increased Special Taxes. Proposition 41 also requires the State Auditor to periodically review programs that receive funding from special taxes created or increased by the Legislature or by voters after January 1, 2026. These ongoing audits would happen every four years. Proposition 41 specifies what the State Auditor will include in these audits, including recommendations to improve program efficiency. Proposition 41 specifies that the costs of this ongoing work will be paid using the new tax revenue.
State Appropriations Limit. The State Constitution limits how much tax revenues the state can spend each year. The limit applies to both General Fund taxes and special taxes. However, certain types of spending, for example for infrastructure, are excluded from this limit. Under Proposition 41, the state might not be able to exclude new special tax spending from the limit.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Auditor Costs, Mostly Paid by New Revenues. Proposition 41 would increase State Auditor costs by creating new and ongoing audit requirements. The costs would depend on (1) the number of new or increased special taxes that are proposed and approved and (2) the complexity of the programs being audited. These costs likely would be in the range of the low millions of dollars per year but would grow over time. The one-time and ongoing audit costs associated with special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature would be paid from the revenues collected by the special taxes. One-time audit costs associated with special taxes that do not ultimately appear on the ballot or are rejected by voters would be paid from the state’s General Fund. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.)
Higher Costs to Print and Mail VIG. Proposition 41 would require a summary of the State Auditor’s review to appear in the VIG when a voter initiative with a special tax appears on the ballot. These audit summaries could add several pages to the VIG, which would increase state printing and mailing costs by a few hundred thousand dollars per qualified initiative.
Possible Savings if State Auditor Recommendations Are Implemented. Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to make recommendations for programs to reduce costs or improve efficiency. Proposition 41 could result in savings or improved services if policymakers implement the State Auditor’s recommendations and those recommendations prove effective. Any resulting savings would depend on future decisions and are not known.
Net Effect Not Known. The net fiscal effect of Proposition 41 is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers.

PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
OFFICIAL TITLE AND SUMMARY
PREPARED BY THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
Prohibits any new state taxes that exclude their revenues from the state spending limit approved by voters in 1979.
For statewide special taxes, requires (1) a pre-election audit of programs that would receive funding from a voter-proposed special tax, and (2) recurring audits of programs funded by special taxes enacted after January 1, 2026.
States that other voter-approved measures appearing on the same ballot are void if they conflict with this measure and this measure receives more affirmative votes.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST'S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT:
Unknown net fiscal effect. Increased costs for the California State Auditor to implement new one-time and ongoing audit requirements of programs funded by special taxes. These costs would be mostly paid from the new revenues collected from the special taxes. Possible savings associated with implementing recommendations from the audits.

PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 41
CALIFORNIANS DESERVE BETTER RESULTS FOR OUR TAX DOLLARS
Prop. 41 requires the State Auditor to conduct independent public audits of programs funded by proposed new taxes in order to increase transparency and accountability and drive better outcomes.
Californians pay some of the highest taxes in the country-on top of our high cost of living. This year alone, California’s state government will spend more than $350 billion-a 79% increase in spending since 2019. Billions of our tax dollars have flowed into state programs like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it.
We deserve better education, health care, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned money we pay to the state.
Prop. 41 requires more accountability, transparency and trackable progress of programs funded by our taxes, so that we stop funding failure and start funding successful outcomes.
Here’s how Prop. 41 works.
PUBLIC AUDITS TO PROVIDE ACCOUNTABILITY, TRANSPARENCY AND OVERSIGHT
Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct performance and financial audits of the programs funded by new tax measures, with the results posted publicly. The audits must:
• Track all program spending and assess whether it’s achieving its intended outcomes; • Determine whether programs have sufficient oversight and accountability; • Identify areas of waste, fraud and abuse; • Recommend how future waste and fraud can be avoided and programs made more effective.

nonpartisan research institute concluded that

income taxes, sales taxes, property taxes, and other
forms of taxation. California has the highest state sales
tax in the nation, the highest top income tax rate, and
the highest tax on gasoline, among other indicators.

including to children, families, and the most vulnerable
in our state. But billions of our tax dollars have flowed
into programs like homelessness efforts, with far too
little to show for it.

hard-earned money to support programs that are
ineffective, we must institute greater transparency and
trackable progress of program improvements to ensure
we stop funding failure and start funding successful
outcomes. Government must use our tax dollars more
wisely.

Constitutional Amendment
Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues From State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes.
Requires audits of citizen initiatives for special taxes. Imposes spending limits on all new special taxes.
SPUR's Recommendation
More transparency and accountability in government spending are worthy objectives. However, the Legislative Analyst’s Office and the state auditor already have the authority to evaluate policies and programs to ensure they are equitable and efficient. Prop. 41 was primarily placed on the ballot to defeat Prop. 40, a measure to tax billionaires. In addition, it would constrain local and state governments’ ability to raise revenue now and in the future for much-needed housing, transportation, infrastructure, and social services, which are already facing cuts at the federal and state levels.
Vote NO
What Prop. 41 Would Do
Proposition 41 would require the state auditor, working with the Legislative Analyst’s Office, to conduct an independent review of any state-level citizen initiative that aims to create a new special tax once it reaches 25% of the required signature threshold to be placed on the ballot. (Special taxes differ from general taxes in that they dedicate revenue to a specific purpose.) All new state-level special taxes would be audited every four years.
Additionally, any new special taxes passed after January 1, 2026 — whether proposed through legislation or through voter initiatives — would be subject to the Gann Limit, a voter-imposed revenue spending limit explained in the Backstory section below.
The audit of proposed citizen initiatives would examine the individual programs that would receive funding through the special tax and assess whether the programs are sufficiently cost-efficient in their hiring and operating practices. It would recommend how the programs could save 10% of their costs. The audit information would be included in the voter information guide, which would increase printing and mailing costs by a few hundred thousand dollars per initiative, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
If a special tax passes, the state auditor would be required to conduct audits every four years to assess spending, evaluate efficiency, and recommend improvements. The auditor would consider public input when measuring the program’s effectiveness. The revenues generated would cover implementation costs. However, the state would pay the initial audit cost if voters rejected the special tax.
Prop. 41 is a countermeasure to the so-called billionaire tax, Prop. 40 (https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/ca-prop-40-billionaire-tax). If both measures pass, the one receiving more votes would prevail.
The Backstory
Special taxes are taxes whose revenues are dedicated to a specific purpose rather than contributing to the state’s general fund budget. The State Legislature can levy special taxes with two-thirds voter approval, or an initiative placed on the ballot by voter signatures can do so with a simple majority (50% plus one vote). Currently, special taxes have no audit requirements or spending caps.
Since the late 1970s, California has faced numerous tax limitations through Prop. 13 and other constitutional amendments. The Gann Limit imposes requirements on how the state can spend General Fund revenues. If the state’s revenues exceed the Gann Limit — a dollar amount based on the state’s spending level in 1978–1979, adjusted for population and per capita income — half of revenues over the limit must be allocated to K–14 education and the other half returned to taxpayers. 1 Historically, the Gann Limit has rarely affected distribution of the state’s revenues, but if the state experiences strong income gains (including business/corporate/stock gains) over the limit, it could result in decreasing investment in state priorities such as housing, health care, economic development, and infrastructure.
The fiscal impacts of Prop. 41 are unknown. Adding pages to the voter information guide would cost money, but the audits could also create savings. If this measure prevents the state from raising new revenues from future taxes, it could have a significant negative fiscal impact in the longer term.
Prop. 41 is a countermeasure to Prop. 40, a one-time special tax on individuals with more than $1 billion in assets. Prop. 40 is intended to offset federal funding cuts to critical social safety net programs, including Medi-Cal, CalFresh, and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. The revenues generated from Prop. 40 would be exempt from the Gann Limit.
Prop. 41 was placed on the ballot through a signature-gathering effort led by Building a Better California, which is funded by Google co-founder Sergey Brin and other billionaires. It requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass. If it passes with more votes than Prop. 40, it would nullify Prop. 40. (Building a Better California has also placed Prop. 42 (https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/ca-prop-42-personal-property-taxes), a separate countermeasure to Prop. 40, on the ballot.)
Equity Impacts
Restricting spending from special taxes could negatively affect efforts to fund health care, food assistance, and other programs that disproportionately benefit lower-income Californians and communities of color.
Pro
Audits of proposed citizen initiatives could help ensure that the programs they would fund are cost-effective.
Cons
Prop. 41 was placed on the ballot to prevent a competing measure from succeeding. It could affect the state’s ability to raise revenue from other tax measures in the future.
Applying spending limits to new revenue measures could constrain local and state governments’ ability to fund urgent priorities amid unprecedented federal and state budget cuts.
Vote NO

Proposition 41: Audits For New State Special Taxes
Proposition 41: Audits For New State Special Taxes
Proposition 41: Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues From State Spending Limit. Requires Audits For New State Special Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Tax Audits, One-Time Wealth Tax for State-Funded Health Care Programs Initiative.
Improving Transparency, Effectiveness, and Efficiency in California Government Act of 2026
The Transparency Act
Summary
Proposition 41 was placed on the ballot by petition signatures to amend the California Constitution. It began as Initiative #25-0041A (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0040A1%20%28Gov.%20Efficiency%29.pdf) , filed with the California Attorney General’s Office. Prop. 41 amends the California Constitution by adding Article XXIV, creating audit review requirements for special tax measures and enforcing state appropriation limits (the Gann Limit) for all future state tax measures.
Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to conduct a financial and performance audit of any citizen initiative proposing a new special tax once the campaign collects 25% of required signatures. The auditor must review specific criteria set by Proposition 41, including identifying ways to cut the proposed program’s annual costs by 10%. If the measure qualifies, an executive summary of the audit is published in the official voter information pamphlet.
Additionally, the State Auditor will conduct ongoing audits every four years for programs receiving funding from special taxes created or increased by the Legislature or voters after January 1, 2026.
Proposition 41 specifies that the costs of these audits will be reimbursed using revenue generated from the new tax if voters approve the measure. If a special tax initiative fails, the state general fund covers the audit costs.
It would also prohibit the state from enforcing any new tax enacted or effective on or after January 1, 2026, that is exempted or excluded from the state spending limit.
Proposition 41 conflicts directly with Proposition 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/index.htm) (the Billionaire Wealth Tax initiative). If both pass, whichever measure receives more "yes" votes will prevail in its entirety. Because Proposition 40 excludes its revenues from the state spending limit, Proposition 41 would render Proposition 40 unenforceable if Proposition 41 wins more votes.
Note about the Gann Limit: Approved by California voters in 1979 asProposition 4 (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/ca_ballot_props/864/), the Gann Limit restricts how much tax revenue state and local governments (including school districts) can spend each year, adjusted annually for population changes and economic growth. The limit applies to both General Fund taxes (unrestricted funds for general government operations) and special taxes (funds earmarked for specific purposes), though certain spending categories—such as infrastructure and emergency response—are exempt. (Sources: California Budget Center, What is the Gann Limit? (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians) , Gann Limit (Wikipedia) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gann_Limit) , CA Department of Finance, Description of (https://dof.ca.gov/media/docs/budget/california-budget-frequently-asked-questions/fundclassifications.pdf)Fund Classifications in the Treasury (https://dof.ca.gov/media/docs/budget/california-budget-frequently-asked-questions/fundclassifications.pdf))
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
The net fiscal effect of Proposition 41 is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers. However, the State Auditor costs will increase due to the new and ongoing work to carry out the audit requirements in this measure.
Due to additional pages of audit information being included in the voter information guides could increase state printing and mailing costs by a few hundred thousand dollars per qualified initiative on the ballot.
What your vote means (LAO Analysis)
YES: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
NO: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that Proposition 41 improves transparency and reduces government waste by requiring independent state audits of programs funded by new special taxes while ensuring all state taxes respect voter-approved spending caps, as detailed in the Official Voter Information Guide.
Opponents contend that the measure was put on the ballot by billionaire opponents to block Prop. 40, a proposed wealth tax on billionaires, and that its audit requirements create unnecessary hurdles to funding essential public services like healthcare and education.

More Transparency.
More Accountability.
​
Better Results for Our Tax Dollars.
1/3
​ Yes on Proposition 41: Audits and Accountability for California Tax Dollars.
​
Billions of our tax dollars have flowed into state programs like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it. Californians deserve better education, healthcare, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned money we pay to the state.
​
Proposition 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct financial and performance audits of the programs funded by any new tax measure, with results posted publicly. It also requires that all new taxes comply with the state's voter-approved spending limit - so that excess tax revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
If approved by voters, Prop 41 would require ongoing public audits to evaluate spending, identify waste, fraud or abuse, assess whether they are meeting their intended goals, and recommend improvements.
Learn More About Prop 41 (https://www.yesonprop41.org/about-prop41)
Endorsements
YES on Prop 41 is supported by a growing coalition of small businesses, taxpayers, good government advocates, elected officials, accountants and auditing experts.
Prop 41 is also supported by more than a million Californians who helped qualify the measure for the ballot.
Our Coalition (https://www.yesonprop41.org/)
"California families pay billions in state taxes every year and they deserve to see where that money goes and what it delivers. Proposition 41 brings real accountability and clear metrics to state spending. We're proud to support it."
Tracy Hernandez, Co-Founder and CEO of the New California Coalition
"This commonsense, long overdue reform will finally instill some transparency and accountability in state spending - ensuring Californians get better government services for the taxes we pay. It provides an independent, public report card for government spending, so government programs work better for everyone."
​
Pat Fong Kushida, President/CEO of the CalAsian Chamber
"Californians are paying more for everything, including some of the highest taxes in the country. Now more than ever, Californians deserve some relief from our state's high taxes. Prop 41 delivers."
​
Steve Westly, former Controller of California
California can't afford to keep funding programs with no accountability.
Current and former public auditors and a growing list of California residents and transparency advocates support Prop 41. Add your name to the list and join us in promoting greater accountability and better results.

Vote NO on Props 41 and 42: the billionaire-funded tricks to undo Prop 40
Introduced by Healthcare Workers
Prop 40, The California Billionaire Tax
Proposition 40 is a one-time, 5% tax on billionaires. It demands that the ultra-wealthy pay their fair share to help protect healthcare for all Californians.
Trump slashed healthcare funding to give tax breaks to the richest Americans. The impacts: skyrocketing health insurance premiums, 3.4 million Californians losing health coverage, and clinics, ERs, and hospitals closing their doors.
Prop 40 restores this lost funding, stopping cost increases and ensuring Californians can get the care we need.
Billionaires like Sergey Brin and Peter Thiel are spending tens of millions in non-stop ads attacking Prop 40. They think they can fool us into voting no. But millions of Californians are about to prove them wrong.
Vote YES to finally tax billionaires.
How to Tax the Billionaires (https://yeson40.com/vote-yes-on-40/)
Facts on Prop 40 (https://yeson40.com/facts/%20)
Get Involved (https://yeson40.com/volunteer/)
Who’s Taking a Stand to Tax the Billionaires
See the full list (https://yeson40.com/endorsements/)
The Solution to the Crisis
How Prop 40 Will Help California.
Proposition 40 is a one-time, 5% tax only on Californians worth more than $1 billion—around 200 of the wealthiest people in the world. The other 39 million Californians will pay nothing.
Facts on Prop 40 (https://yeson40.com/facts/%20)
The Initiative (https://yeson40.com/the-initiative/%20)
The Crisis is Here.
We’re paying more because billionaires insist on paying less.
Read more
Loopholes and tax breaks let billionaires pay only a tiny amount in state income tax – about 0.2% of their wealth (https://eml.berkeley.edu/~saez/BSZ26CAbillionaires.pdf) – lower rates than most California working families. Trump gave them even more breaks and stuck the rest of us with the bill.
Healthcare costs keep rising—for all of us.
Read more
Working Californians are already struggling with the steep costs of healthcare. Trump’s federal funding cuts are pushing our premiums even higher. Up to 3.4 million Californians (https://ahea.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-01/ca-budget-and-policy-center-impact-of-federal-funding-cuts-2-pager.pdf) will lose access to coverage altogether.
Healthcare facilities are already closing.
Read more
Massive federal cuts have caused 7 clinics in Los Angeles County (http://publichealth.lacounty.gov/phcommon/public/media/mediapubhpdetail.cfm?prid=5253) to shut their doors. Another 83 hospitals and clinics (https://www.citizen.org/article/big-ugly-threat/) in California are at-risk of closing. It will be harder for all of us to get care when we need it.
How Prop 40 Helps California.
Protects access and limits price increases.
Read more
Allows 3.4 million Californian (https://ahea.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-01/ca-budget-and-policy-center-impact-of-federal-funding-cuts-2-pager.pdf)s to keep their health insurance and millions more not see their premiums skyrocket.
Keeps local hospitals and ERs open.
Read more
Restores lost federal funds that hospitals, clinics, nursing homes, and home care services rely on, ensuring millions of children, seniors, veterans, and families can access care.
Funds public schools and food assistance.
Read more
Prevents teacher layoffs in public schools and keeps kids and families fed through food assistance programs.
Vote NO on 41 & 42 (https://votenoon41and42.com/)
These initiatives are designed to trick voters into undoing Proposition 40. Don’t be fooled: Props 41 and 42 aren’t about helping California. They were put on the ballot because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share.

Proposition 41
Require audits of new tax programs
This proposition would make it harder to pass new special taxes by requiring the state auditor to review any special tax proposal before it goes to voters. The auditor would assess whether the program that would receive funding could cut spending by at least 10% annually. Any new special tax approved by voters would count toward California’s spending limit, potentially triggering automatic refunds that reduce funding for other state programs. If this proposition receives more votes than Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) (a wealth tax on billionaires), Proposition 40 is nullified, even if Proposition 40 also passes. It was placed on the ballot by opponents of the proposed billionaire tax.

What Would Proposition 41 Mean for California?
Understanding the Proposed Audit Requirements for Special Taxes and the Prohibition on Excluding Revenues from the State Spending Limit
September 2026 | By Kayla Kitson (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/kayla-kitson/)
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Prop. 41 would 1) impose new audit requirements for programs funded with state special taxes and 2) prohibit the collection of new state taxes that are excluded from the state’s spending limit. The primary intent of the measure is to invalidate Prop. 40 — the billionaire tax also appearing on the November ballot — but Prop. 41 could also make it harder for the state to meet the needs of Californians in the future.
What Would Prop. 41 Do?
Prop. 41 would amend the state Constitution to impose new rules related to state taxes. The measure would require “financial and performance audits” of programs receiving revenues from special taxes and would also prevent state taxes from being excluded from California’s spending cap, also known as the “Gann Limit.”
Creates New Audit Requirements for Special Taxes
Prop. 41 would create new pre-election and ongoing audit requirements for programs receiving — or proposed to receive — revenues from state-level special taxes. In contrast to a general tax, which can be used for any purpose, a special tax raises revenue for specific purposes.
Pre-election audits: The State Auditor would be required to perform an audit of any program that would be funded by a special tax proposed through a statewide voter initiative. The audit would be required while the initiative is being circulated for signatures — before it officially qualifies for the ballot — and a summary of the audit findings would be included in the voter information guide. The full audit would also be made available to the public.
Ongoing audits: The State Auditor would be required to audit programs receiving revenues from special taxes enacted by the Legislature or approved by voters through a statewide initiative on or after January 1, 2026. These audits would be required every four years.
The audits would assess programs based on specific criteria outlined in Prop. 41, and would require the State Auditor to recommend how programs could reduce costs by at least 10% annually.
The State Auditor would be reimbursed for the costs of these audits with revenues from the relevant special tax. If, however, a special tax initiative fails to qualify for the ballot or is rejected by voters, the audit costs would be absorbed by the state’s General Fund.
Prohibits Taxes That Are Excluded from the State Spending Limit
Prop. 41 would prevent the state from collecting or enforcing any state tax that is 1) enacted on or after January 1, 2026 and 2) excluded from the state spending cap, also known as the Gann Limit (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians/). Currently, the measure would apply only to Prop. 40 if both measures pass and Prop. 41 receives more votes, but it could potentially be applied to other tax policy proposals in the future.
California’s spending limit was established by Prop. 4 (1979) and is based on state spending in 1978-79, annually adjusted for population changes and inflation. Under the state Constitution, if state revenues exceed the limit over two consecutive years, the excess must be split equally between refunds to taxpayers and spending on TK-14 education. In effect, the spending limit restricts the ability of state leaders to raise and spend revenue to meet the most pressing needs of Californians.
Conflicts with Other Measures on the Ballot
The California Constitution states that if provisions of multiple measures on the same ballot conflict, the provisions of the measure receiving the higher number of votes will prevail. Prop. 41 broadly specifies that if another measure on the same ballot either 1) imposes different audit rules on special taxes or 2) contains a tax that is exempted from the state spending limit, the entirety of the other measure would be invalidated if Prop. 41 receives more votes.
Prop. 41 is in direct conflict with Prop. 40. (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/) This is because Prop. 40 would create a one-time tax on the wealth of billionaires and exclude the revenues from the state spending limit, which Prop. 41 prohibits.
If both measures were to be approved and Prop. 41 received more votes, Prop. 40 could be invalidated. Alternatively, if both measures pass but Prop. 40 receives more votes, the billionaire tax could be collected, but it is possible that audits would be required of Medi-Cal and other programs receiving Prop. 40 dollars. If both measures pass, there may be litigation regarding the application of conflicting provisions, and the final decision would be made by the courts.
How Would Prop. 41 Affect Californians and the State Budget?
The primary intent of Prop. 41 is to invalidate the Prop. 40 billionaire tax, but it would also create new barriers to raising state revenue and effectively meeting the needs of Californians.
Prop. 41 would also increase state costs related to conducting audits for programs that are often already subject to close scrutiny — reducing funding available to support critical state services. This would come at a time when Californians are already dealing with affordability concerns as well as the consequences of the steep federal cuts to health care and food assistance enacted in H.R. 1 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/timeline-of-funding-cuts-to-medi-cal-and-calfresh-in-california/), signed by President Trump in 2025.
Impacts of Audit Requirements
The pre-election audit requirement could dissuade voters from approving special tax initiatives that would raise needed revenue to support and improve state services that help Californians stay healthy, housed, and economically secure. A summary of the audit would appear in the voter guide, and voters could interpret it as evidence that the programs to be funded are inefficient or ineffective. For example, because the State Auditor would be required to recommend options to cut program costs by 10%, voters may assume this means the program is inefficient even if that is not the case.
Additionally, the requirement for cost-cutting recommendations could result in service cuts with real human impacts. While policymakers would be under no obligation to implement these recommendations, if they did it could result in cuts to core services rather than simply “inefficient spending.” For example, if a program receiving special tax revenues is already operating efficiently but the Auditor must identify ways that costs could be reduced by 10%, lawmakers may be under pressure to adopt those recommendations — particularly in difficult budget times. Those cuts could lead to fewer Californians being served, reductions in benefit levels, or decreased service quality.
While it is clearly important for tax dollars to be spent efficiently and effectively, many state programs are already subject to occasional or ongoing audits. The State Auditor currently performs audits as a result of (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/about-us/#where-our-work-comes-from) existing state laws, legislative requests, and whistleblower tips. Additionally, the “High-Risk” audit program requires the Auditor to periodically review programs or agencies determined to be at high risk for “waste, fraud, abuse, or mismanagement” or those raising concerns related to efficiency or effectiveness.
Prop. 41’s additional audits would increase state costs, reducing the resources available to directly support services for Californians. Moreover, in the case of program audits related to a proposed special tax, the audit costs would be absorbed by the state’s General Fund if the ballot initiative were not enacted, leaving less funding for critical state services like education, health care, and human services.
Impacts of State Spending Limit Provisions
The primary impact of preventing new revenues from being excluded from the spending limit would be the invalidation of the billionaire tax proposed by Prop. 40 — if both measures pass and Prop. 41 receives more votes.
In the future, voters may be able to exclude the revenues from a statewide tax initiative from the spending cap if the initiative amends the Constitution to do so. In fact, previous initiatives have explicitly excluded new tax revenues from the limit, such as tobacco taxes enacted under Prop. 10 (1998) and Prop. 56 (2016). However, legal challenges are possible and there is no certainty on how courts would rule.
State policymakers already lack the authority to exclude new tax revenues from the spending cap without voter approval because the cap is enshrined in the state Constitution.
There are some existing state revenue streams that could potentially be affected by Prop. 41, but there are many complications and uncertainties and any conflicts would ultimately be decided by the courts. For example, some health care financing sources that must be occasionally reauthorized — such as the Managed Care Organization (MCO) tax and the Hospital Quality Assurance fee, which both allow the state to draw down additional federal funding for Medi-Cal — could potentially be impacted by Prop. 41. This, in turn, would jeopardize billions of dollars in federal funding for Medi-Cal at a time when Californians are already experiencing the harms of the deep federal cuts to health care resulting from H.R. 1.
Who Supports and Opposes Prop. 41?
The top contributor to the Prop. 41 campaign is a group called “Building a Better California,” which is largely funded (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1486767&view=received) by Google cofounder Sergey Brin and other billionaires. This same group is also opposing Prop. 40 and supporting Prop. 42. Prop. 41 is also endorsed by the California Republican Party, the California Chamber of Commerce, and the California Taxpayers Association.
There is no official campaign against Prop. 41. However, prominent opponents include the Service Employees International Union – United Health Workers West (SEIU–UHW) — the main proponent of the Prop. 40 billionaire tax measure — as well as other labor groups including the California Federation of Teachers and the California Federation of Labor Unions. The California Democratic Party and the League of Women Voters also oppose Prop. 41.

Frequently Asked Questions About Proposition 41
Q: What does Prop 41 do?
A: Prop 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct public performance and financial audits of programs funded by proposed new taxes, bringing government transparency and accountability to spending decisions before voters make them.
Californians pay some of the highest taxes in the country - on top of our high cost of living. Billions of our tax dollars have flowed into state programs, like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it. We deserve better education, healthcare, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned money we pay to the state.
Proposition 41 (2026) puts independent audits and measurable outcomes at the center of how California funds programs with new tax dollars, so that we stop funding failure and start funding successful outcomes.
Q: Does Prop 41 raise taxes?
A: No. Prop 41 does not create or increase any taxes - it protects taxpayers' interests by:
1) Identifying shortcomings in programs and recommending fixes, to help deliver better results for our taxes;
Reducing the waste and fraud that have cost California taxpayers billions of dollars in recent years; and
Requires all taxes to comply with the state's voter-approved spending limit - including its requirement that excess revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
Prop 41 ensures taxpayers get better results, not just a bigger tax bill.
Q: How do the audits work?
Proposition 41 requires the independent California State Auditor to review programs that would be funded by a new or higher special tax proposed to California voters. The first review happens before the tax reaches the ballot. Once a special tax initiative collects 25 percent of the signatures needed to qualify, the State Auditor audits each program that would receive the money, looking at whether the program is achieving its goals, how well it spends its dollars, and where fraud, waste, or abuse may exist. A summary of the findings is printed in the Voter Information Guide so voters can read it before they vote. If a new special tax is approved by voters, the State Auditor reviews the funded programs again every four years and invites public input.
The audits produce findings and recommendations, and both are public. Decisions about funding stay with voters and the Legislature, as they are today, and the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst Office notes that acting on the recommendations "could result in savings or improved
services at existing funding levels." A program funded by a new special tax is reviewed before any change to its funding is made. For a full walkthrough, see the our explainer here (https://www.yesonprop41.org/how-audits-work) .
Q: Who conducts the audits?
A: The audits are conducted by California's independent State Auditor, the state's nonpartisan fiscal watchdog, and shared broadly with the public, including in the Voter Information Guide. The financial and performance audits must:
Track all program spending and assess whether it's achieving its intended outcomes;
Determine whether programs have sufficient oversight and accountability;
Identify areas of waste, fraud and abuse; and,
Recommend how future waste and fraud can be avoided and how programs can be made more effective.
Under Prop 41, the Auditor is required to review programs funded by proposed new tax measures before voters cast their ballots and conduct ongoing audits if those measures are approved.
Q: What happens if an audit finds problems?
A: If the State Auditor identifies concerns about oversight, accountability or program performance, those findings are included in the Voter Information Guide so voters can make a more informed decision.
If a measure is approved, future audits continue evaluating how funds are spent, identify areas for improvement, and recommend ways to make programs more effective over time - so that programs are held accountable to the people who pay for them: taxpayers.
The audit doesn't decide whether a measure passes or fails; it gives voters independent information before they cast their ballot.
Q: What does Prop 41 mean for education, healthcare and other public programs?
A: Every tax dollar we waste is a dollar that could actually help someone. Prop 41 is built to sustain fiscal discipline alongside public investment. It does not cut or eliminate funding for education, healthcare or other public services, and it helps ensure that programs funded by taxpayers are transparent, accountable and delivering results. We deserve better services in return for the hard-earned money we pay to the state.
Prop 41 requires more accountability, transparency and trackable progress of programs funded by our taxes, like homelessness (https://www.yesonprop41.org/homelessness) , so that we stop funding failure and start funding successful outcomes.
Q: Does Prop 41 make it harder for initiatives to qualify for the ballot?
A: No. Prop 41 does not change the initiative process or prevent measures from qualifying for the ballot. Supporters can still gather signatures, qualify initiatives and campaign for their proposals just as they do today.
The difference is that under Prop 41, programs to be funded by new taxes are assessed before voters cast their ballot. The Auditor's findings must be posted in the Voter Information Guide, so voters have access to independent information about how programs are being managed and whether they actually need more funding. Voters deserve the ability to make informed decisions about new taxes without having to rely on information from special interests or politicians.
Q: Who pays for the audits?
A: If a tax measure is approved, the cost of the required audits is paid from the revenues generated by that measure. If voters reject the measure, the audit costs are paid through the state's General Fund.
Many statewide tax measures raise hundreds of millions - or even billions - of dollars over time. Prop 41 ensures a small investment in independent oversight helps taxpayers know whether those dollars are being spent effectively and producing the results promised.
Q: Who supports Prop 41?
Prop 41 is backed by a board coalition of small businesses, taxpayers, good government advocates, accountants, and auditing experts. Endorsers include the California Society of Certified Public Accountants, former State Controller Steve Westly, former California Auditor General Tom Hayes, the NAACP California-Hawaii State Conference, the California Alliance of Seniors, the California Chamber of Commerce, the California Farm Bureau, the California Taxpayers Association, the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, along with dozens of local chambers, taxpayer associations, and regional economic partnerships across the state.
Endorsements also include Democratic organizations and officials. The Chinese American Democratic Club, the San Bernardino Young Democrats, and the Sacramento State College Democrats have endorsed Prop 41, as has Steve Westly, a Democrat who served as State Controller. Local officials who have endorsed include Riverside County Auditor-Controller Ben Benoit and council members and mayors from across California. The full and current list of endorsers is at yesonprop41.org/endorsements (https://www.yesonprop41.org/endorsements) .
Q: How does Prop 41 strengthen taxpayer protections?
A: Prop 41 requires all future state tax measures to comply with California's voter-approved constitutional spending limit. That means future measures must follow the same constitutional rules that already apply to state spending including the requirement that excess revenues be refunded to taxpayers when the spending limit is exceeded.
Prop 41 provides for consistent application of the spending limit, so future state tax measures follow the same constitutional rules that already govern state spending, including the requirement that excess revenues be refunded to taxpayers.

What does California Proposition 41 do?
This proposition would make it harder to pass new special taxes by requiring the state auditor to review any special tax proposal before it goes to voters. The auditor would assess whether the program that would receive funding could cut spending by at least 10% annually. Any new special tax approved by voters would count toward California’s spending limit, potentially triggering automatic refunds that reduce funding for other state programs. If this proposition receives more votes than Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) (a wealth tax on billionaires), Proposition 40 is nullified, even if Proposition 40 also passes.

What do supporters and opponents say?
Supporters
Arguments for
Supporters say key social programs are not getting enough funding despite California’s high taxes. They argue the state auditor should assess whether the programs that would benefit from special taxes are spending money wisely. Supporters also want these special taxes to count toward the state spending limit, making tax rebates to Californians more likely.

Opponents
Arguments against
The chief opponent is SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, the sponsor of Proposition 40. The union argues that Prop. 41 is designed to trick voters into unknowingly blocking a wealth tax on billionaires. Prop. 41 isn’t about auditing waste in public programs, the union says; instead, it’s a way for billionaires to avoid paying taxes once on their huge wealth.

PROP 41: Special-Tax Audits and the Spending-Limit Lock
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California%20Decides_Proposition%2041.pdf)
Research
Quick Facts
Key Questions
California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Summary
Proposition 41 would write two rules into the California Constitution. First, programs funded by new state special taxes would face independent audits by the state auditor. These audits would occur when the ballot initiative is initially proposed and then every four years after a special tax takes effect. Second, no new state tax could circumvent the Gann limit, the voter-approved spending cap adopted in 1979. Hoover Institution research shows that California’s spending has grown far faster than inflation or population and that the state budget rises and falls with the fortunes of a small number of high-income taxpayers. Proposition 41 is best read as an attempt to restore discipline to that budget. It also contains a clause that, if it outpolls Proposition 40, would void the billionaire tax on the same ballot (see California Decides, Prop 40: The Billionaire Tax Act (https://www.hoover.org/proposition-lab-proposition-40)).
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues from State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.”
Measure’s own name: The Improving Transparency, Effectiveness, and Efficiency in California Government Act of 2026 (AG No. 25-0040A1).
Type: Initiated constitutional amendment.
A vote YES means: Starting retroactively on January 1, 2026, any program that would be the recipient of new or increased special tax revenues as a result of a citizen initiative must undergo state performance audits prior to the vote. Such programs, and those receiving revenues from legislatively enacted new or increased special taxes, must be audited every four years thereafter. No new state tax or increase to a state tax enacted on or after that date may route its revenue outside California’s voter-approved spending limit, commonly referred to as the Gann limit.
A vote NO means: California keeps current law. New special taxes are not subject to this audit regime, and new taxes may continue to direct revenue into funds that sit outside the Gann limit, as several existing taxes already do.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0040A1, Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0040A1%20(Gov.%20Efficiency).pdf)
LAO analysis: Ballot analysis of Initiative 25-0040 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-040)
1. Overview
Proposition 41 would add a new Article XXIV, titled “Protecting Taxpayer Dollars,” to the California Constitution. It has two main provisions.
The first provision is an audit requirement for programs that would receive funds from proposed special tax initiatives. A special tax is one whose revenue is dedicated to specific purposes rather than available for general use. When the proponents of a citizen initiative that would create a new or increased special tax notify the secretary of state that they have gathered 25 percent of the required signatures, the state auditor must begin a financial and performance audit of each program the special tax would fund. The audit must assess program effectiveness, evaluate the potential for fraud, waste, and abuse, and recommend ways the program could achieve budgetary savings of at least 10 percent a year. If the measure qualifies for the ballot, an executive summary of the audit must be printed in the state voter information guide.
A subsequent audit must be repeated every four years for every new or increased special tax enacted by the legislature or by voters on or after January 1, 2026. When a tax passes, the audit costs are reimbursed from the tax’s own revenue. When a tax initiative fails to qualify or is rejected, the general fund absorbs the cost.
The second provision protects the state spending limit from being circumvented by future state taxes. The Gann limit, adopted by voters as Proposition 4 in 1979 and amended by Proposition 111 in 1990, caps how much tax revenue the state may appropriate each year. It’s adjusted for increases to population and per capita income, and some substantial categories of spending are excluded from the cap. According to the Gann limit, if tax revenue exceeds the limit over two consecutive years the excess revenue must be split between taxpayer rebates and additional K–14 school funding. For context, rapid tax revenue growth has rarely resulted in mandatory Gann limit rebates.
However, under current rules a new tax can be written to deposit its revenue in a fund that is excluded from the appropriations counted against the Gann limit. Proposition 41 would forbid that design for any state tax enacted by the legislature or by voter initiative, but the ban is limited to taxes that take effect on or after January 1, 2026. New special taxes would still be permitted, but their revenue would simply count toward the same spending cap that applies to other nonexempt tax revenues.
The second provision connects Proposition 41 to Proposition 40, the Billionaire Tax Act. If Prop 40 is approved it would route its revenue into a separate reserve fund that sits outside the structure of the Gann limit, the Proposition 98 school-funding guarantee, and the rainy-day budget rules. Proposition 41 prohibits new or increased state taxes from circumventing the structure intended to limit the growth of California government spending, and it includes specific text that will nullify Proposition 40 if both initiatives pass but Proposition 41 receives more yes votes.
2. The legal language
Full text:
Initiative 25-0040A1, “The Improving Transparency, Effectiveness, and Efficiency in California Government Act of 2026,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0040A1%20(Gov.%20Efficiency).pdf) (eight pages, amended language submitted January 12, 2026).
Key language:
“No state tax that is enacted or takes effect on or after January 1, 2026 shall be exempted or excluded from the Government Spending Limitation. The State of California shall not impose, collect, or enforce any state tax that is enacted or takes effect on or after January 1, 2026 if the state tax is exempted or excluded from the Government Spending Limitation.”
What it amends: Adds a new Article XXIV, titled “Protecting Taxpayer Dollars,” to the California Constitution. The article defines “Government Spending Limitation” as Article XIII B, the Gann limit, and defines an exempted tax as one whose revenue is deposited outside the general fund and left out of the appropriations subject to the limit or that raises the appropriations limit by statute.
Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot repeal it. The measure also includes a self-defense provision that appoints and funds independent counsel through a continuous general fund appropriation if the governor and attorney general decline to defend it.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
What?
It would create constitutionally required audits of programs funded by new or increased special taxes, both before a tax initiative reaches voters and every four years after a tax takes effect. It also creates a ban on excluding the revenue from any new or increased state tax from the Gann spending limit.
Where?
Statewide, written into the California Constitution.
When?
It takes effect on passage and reaches back to taxes enacted or effective on or after January 1, 2026.
Why?
The initiative’s authors frame it as a response to California’s nation-leading tax rates and their effect on the state’s affordability crisis. The stated purpose is to require up-front, recurring audits of programs funded by special taxes and to prevent new taxes from circumventing the Gann limit so that surplus revenue is refunded rather than spent.
4. Analysis and Assessment
Audit requirements of Proposition 41 address a documented problem. For example, in 2024 the state auditor found that California spent roughly $24 billion on homelessness and housing programs over five fiscal years without consistently tracking whether the money reduced homelessness. Three of the five programs reviewed did not produce enough data to judge their cost-effectiveness at all. Proposition 41 would make that kind of review routine for programs funded by new special taxes, and it would give voters an audit summary before they vote on a tax initiative. Independent, recurring performance audits with concrete savings targets are the kind of accountability that good-government advocates across the spectrum have long sought.
Proposition 41’s requirement that future special taxes be subject to the Gann limit is similarly reasonable: California’s fiscal challenge is accelerated spending, not a shortage of revenue. Research by Hoover Institution Senior Fellow Lee Ohanian shows that from 2019 to 2023 California’s population fell by almost 500,000 people, while the state budget grew nearly 57 percent (31 percent after inflation). Additional research by Hoover fellows Lanhee J. Chen and Joshua D. Rauh describes how California’s heavy reliance on the personal income tax, which now supplies most general fund tax revenue, ties the budget to the performance of the stock market. In 2021, the top 10 percent of taxpayers paid almost 90 percent of personal income tax revenue. Meanwhile, the state budget swung $175 billion from a surplus in 2022 to a deficit in 2024.
The Gann limit is one of the few constitutional tools that restrains government spending growth during economic booms that becomes a fiscal catastrophe during leaner times. Prior analysis by Hoover Fellow Bill Whalen has traced how the Gann limit’s fiscal discipline has been eroded over time, from Proposition 111’s 1990 exclusion of new gas tax revenue to budgeting practices that kept billions out of the limit calculation. Proposition 41 would close the special-fund circumvention for any future tax.
Importantly, Prop 41 does not ban new taxes, nor does it cut existing programs. It simply requires that revenue from any new tax be counted alongside the rest of state spending, so that a future surplus is dedicated to a tax rebate and additional school funding (per Prop 4 and Prop 111) rather than accumulating in a dedicated fund. This rule should help encourage policymakers to be more thoughtful about expanding government programs when tax revenues unexpectedly increase.
Like Proposition 42, Proposition 41 contains a clause that, if it outpolls Proposition 40, would nullify Prop 40. This specificity is likely preferable to asking the courts to decide which parts of two conflicting constitutional amendments survive.
5. Conclusion
Proposition 41 would require any programs receiving funding from new or increased special taxes to be audited by the state auditor to assess performance, evaluate potential for waste, fraud, and abuse, and identify explicit cost savings opportunities. It would also require each new state tax enacted by the legislature or by voter initiative to be subject to the Gann limit. Its most immediate effect would be to nullify Proposition 40 if it draws more yes votes, while its lasting effect would be to hold all future state taxes to the same spending cap as the rest of the budget.
Hoover Institution research shows that California’s fiscal problem is driven by spending increases that have managed to outstrip even the state’s strong tax revenue growth. From that perspective, Proposition 41 would offer increased oversight on how well California is spending taxpayer dollars.

Endorsement: Yes on Propositions 41 and 42 to limit taxation in California

By The Editorial Board (https://www.ocregister.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)
PUBLISHED: September 21, 2026 at 2:39 PM PDT | UPDATED: September 21, 2026 at 2:56 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
The most hotly debated initiative on the November ballot is Proposition 40, which would impose a 5% tax on the wealth of California billionaires. As this Editorial Board opined (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/13/endorsement-no-on-proposition-40s-reckless-wealth-tax/) in our opposition, the union-created Billionaire Tax Act would send a dangerous message to current and future entrepreneurs, and “have a chilling effect on investment.”
But two closely related measures, Propositions 41 and 42 (https://www.bakersfield.com/opinion/our-view/our-view-vote-no-on-propositions-40-41-42-tax-propositions-hurt-state-californians/article_1c8492b8-5fb9-4897-9f1c-c9ba56460e0d.amp.html) , have received much less attention — partly because they’re so complicated. By adding related measures to the ballot, opponents of Prop. 40 are hoping that voters approve one of these alternatives that will derail Prop. 40. Because these two measures have elements that contradict Prop. 40, the one that gets the highest vote totals (if voters OK them all) would go into effect.
Adding similar-sounding measures also muddies the waters, thus increasing the likelihood that confused voters vote “no” on all of them — thus accomplishing the main goal of stopping the billionaires’ tax. But our goal isn’t to map out political strategies (https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/americanexperience/features/nash-game/) . It’s a worthy effort to try to stop a disastrous new tax scheme.
Besides their intended purpose of blocking Prop. 40, the measures could protect taxpayers for years to come.
Specifically, Prop. 41 would require one-time audits of programs that any proposed special taxes would fund. Those audits, which must be completed before the initiative appears on the ballot, would be required to identify ways that such programs could cut annual costs by 10%, per an analysis (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026) from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
While Prop. 40 exempts itself from state spending limits, Prop. 41 also requires new special-tax revenues to count toward the Gann Limit (https://www.sheehystrategygroup.com/news/2026/3/9/californias-state-appropriations-limit-gann-limit) — the 1979 constitutional amendment that caps the revenue the state can spend each year. The state has passed a number of workarounds over the years, but applying new revenues to this formula would potentially require the return of certain additional tax revenues to taxpayers (https://www.yesonprop41.org/about-prop41) and the earmarking of revenues to infrastructure.
Prop. 42 is more straightforward. Per theLAO (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=42&year=2026), the initiative prohibits “new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.” California doesn’t currently tax the ownership of financial assets and only taxes personal property in a limited way (e.g., vehicle license fees), but the measure’s passage “could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes.” It also limits imposition of retroactive taxes.
So would the Editorial Board support these measures even if they were standalone initiatives? The answers are unequivocal: Yes and yes.

Regarding Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) , California could use better audits of spending programs. It’s a good idea to identify ways to trim existing programs before shoveling more money their way. It is taxpayers’ money, after all. Requiring audits after election officials have collected only 25% of qualifying signatures imposes a relatively costly burden, but those expenses are a rounding error for any major program. We also believe the state should better live up to the terms of the Gann Limit.
Regarding Prop. 42 (https://yesonprop42.org/?&utm_medium=paid-search&utm_content=A18&utm_campaign=YesOn42&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24250385746&gbraid=0AAAABEi2smx27CdnofkbhPlt_FqIHXDrD&gclid=CjwKCAjwq8PVBhAKEiwA2i3SHUyIfjJPNFkY5WqUynwZ9APOIPtTZDTa7v5_wEBmvD8nV21v3IkUbhoCCZ8QAvD_BwE) , we endorse its efforts to limit unreasonable future tax increases. G oing back and raising taxes on past earnings (as Prop. 40 does) before the new law was passed is unseemly. Opponents complain that it ties the hands of future Legislatures, but we’re totally fine with putting certain types of assets outside the revenuers’ grasp.
Vote yes on Propositions 41 and 42.

Endorsement: Prop 41 is a cynical poison pill. And it isn’t the only one on California’s ballot
Prop 41 is one of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
It wouldn’t be a California election without a few petty, revenge-motivated ballot measures.
Proposition 41 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop41-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is one of two poison pill attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax. The measure explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 41 or its cousin initiative Prop 42 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-proposition-42-taxes-22449389.php) pass with a larger number of votes.
Backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php), Prop 41 would require new special taxes that raise money for specific purposes to adhere to state spending rules, while mandating regular audits of the programs they fund.
What’s so bad about ensuring California spends tax revenue wisely?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Well, nothing — if that’s what the measure actually does. But it’s a cheap ruse to nullify Prop 40.
The measure targets an obscure — but extremely consequential — spending rule embedded in California’s Constitution.
Known as the Gann Limit (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4416), that rule prevents the state from spending more money per taxpayer than it did in 1979 — the year voters approved the measure — once adjusted for inflation. Any money the state collects over the limit must be either refunded to taxpayers or spent on certain purposes, such as infrastructure or education.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 41 would prohibit any state tax taking effect on or after Jan. 1, 2026 from sidestepping those requirements. That would neuter Prop 40, which explicitly exempts its one-time 5% wealth tax on billionaires from the Gann Limit to backfill federal healthcare cuts.
Loren Kaye, former president of a California Chamber of Commerce-affiliated think tank and a Prop 41 supporter, told us in an endorsement interview that the measure establishes a “level playing field so that everybody is similarly affected once you reach the limit.”
We agree that budget carveouts generally aren’t a good idea. But the Gann Limit isn’t sacrosanct; there are perfectly legitimate reasons for excluding certain revenues from its rules.
Consider California’s Hospital Quality Assurance Fee Program (https://www.dhcs.ca.gov/providers-partners/hospital-quality-assurance-fee-program-hqaf/), which charges hospitals a fee to unlock matching federal healthcare funds and improve services for low-income patients. These funds are currently exempt from the Gann Limit (https://funds.dof.ca.gov/app/download/3158) — a provision voters approved when they green-lighted Prop 52 in 2016 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=52&year=2016).
But the federal government, which has to approve the tax, could easily demand changes to its structure. If that were to happen and Prop 41 passes, the hospital fee program could arguably be considered a “new” special tax — and thus be subject to the Gann Limit, diverting money away from hospitals, argued David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and Prop 41 opponent.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
California’s financial regulations are impossibly complex after decades of ballot-box budgeting. Adding another restriction is only bound to make things worse.
Meanwhile, Prop 41’s audit requirements are, as Darien Shanske, a UC Davis School of Law professor and Prop 41 opponent, put it, meant to be “the chocolate coating that’s supposed to attract people.”
But they’re largely redundant and would decrease efficiency.
Prop 41 requires the state auditor to evaluate programs that will receive funding from new citizen-proposed special taxes and include its findings in the official voter information guide. But the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office already assesses each ballot initiative’s fiscal and practical impact (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop41-110326.pdf) — including at the 25% signature-gathering threshold Prop 41 identifies — and those analyses are included in the voter guide.
The measure’s ongoing audit requirement could also be counterproductive; tax measures typically contain accountability provisions, and adding an untold number of audits to the already overworked auditor’s office could distract from other critical investigations. Furthermore, Prop 41 directs the state auditor’s office to find 10% annual savings in program costs, which is arbitrary and dilutes the office’s independence.
